BOLD ON& One day in March two blunt gruen leaves - Pushed through the hardened ground, And though the wind was grumbling still Looked cheerily around. And ere a week had passed, a bud - .. Came shyly after them, • ;---'-'l5l And hung like tiny fairy bell, Upon a slender stem, When suddenly the sky grew dark, The snow began to fall, And from beneath the ground the bud • Heard little voices call. "You were in too much haste," they cried, _ "Your pretty dress to don, And now what will you do?" She said, "I mean to just hold on." - And dropping low behind her leaves , Of green she hid from sight, While down the snow fell all the day, And down it fell all night. But when it stopped next morn, the birds Sang greetings to their kin, And bright and warm the sun came out To welcome April in. Then quickly ran the snow away, . - -
Andsport -m it was go

_ The bud her leaves of white uncurled-, She had indeed held on; And "Sister Flowers," she gaily cried, "Here I am safe once more, To show the weaker hearts the way Some one must go before; And though I'm such a tiny thing, I really felt no fear When forth I started that bleak morn To act as pioneer. For well I knew that it was spring In spite of wintry din, And that the blossoms on the trees To grow would soon begin; And well I knew erelong the sun The earth would shine upon, So to myself I softly said, 'Hold on, Snow-drop, hold on.r7 —Harper's:Young People.

lONA, 1885. The quiet clouds within the west Have built white domes above the isles, And o'er the leagues of sea at rest The azure calm of summer smiles. The sheldrake and the eider float In peace along each sandy bay; And softly, with the rock-clove's note, The caverns greet the warmth of day.

The purple beds of deep seaweed Scarce wave their fronds around the Ross; A silence blesses croft and mead, Each sculptured stone and knotted cross. . The lark may sing in sunlit air, And through the clover hum the bees; They yield the only sounds of care Where warred and toiled the pure CuldeeS. And yonder grey square minster tower z • For orisons in silence calls, To where, enshrined in turf aid flower, , Kings guard the ruined chapel walls. --7. lona, "island of the waye," - Faith's ancient fort and armoury, Tomb of the holy and the ba•ave, . Our sires' first pledge of Calvary; Christ's mission soil, 0 sacred sand, That knew His first apostle's' tread! 0 rocks of refuge, whence ,our land • Was first with living waters fed! •• ' Mysteriously Columba's time Foretold "a second deluge dark, • When they who on Thy hill may climb Shall find in Thee their safety's ark. • Though hushed awhile, the hymns of praise _ Again shall rise, where feed the kine." Once more shall o'er thy grassy ways Religion's long processions shine? ! Shall then each morn and evening late Unfolded see the illumined scroll, While echoed over shore and strait The sea-like organ-surges roil? 0 saint and prophet! cloth thy word Foretell an earthly Church's reign, Firm as thine island rocks, unstirred By tempests of the northern main?. Perchance! Thy wasted walls have seen The incense round the altars rise, When cloister, tower, and cell had been To Pagan rage a sacrifioe. But if the old cathedral ne'er Again shall send such children forth, Like those who, with the arms of prayer, Were conquerors of the Pictish north; Yet bath that vanguard set and cast Such light upon our age's tide, That o'er life's trackless ocean vast Secure we sail, or anchored, ride. And pilgrims to his grave shall tell The prophet's mnanuig-where he trod, And in Columba's spirit dwell, , ' • Safe-isled within the fear of God! ,--Good Words. TUB MARQUIS Op LORNE.

Some faiths are like those milli that cannot grind their torn unless they work against the wind.—Quarles. The one doctrine in which all religions agree is, that new light is added to the mind in proportion as it uses that which it has.—R. W. Emerson. "Enveloped in a common mist," wrote George Eliot, "we seem to walk in clearness ourselves, and behold only the mist that enshrouds others." The road of By-and-by leads to the town of ICever. The grave is but a slight elevation, and yet standing on it we see farther than from the highest mountain. "They are never alone," wrote Samuel Smiles, "that are accompanied by holy thoughts. The good and true thought may in time of temptation be as an angel of mercy, purifying and guarding the soul." "It is a part of the selfishness, of human nature," re- marks airbett, "to have a keener memory for sorrow than for joy; the occasional troubles often blot out of remembrance the habitual pleasures; just as we think more of the occasional storm that darkens the sky than of the sun that shines day by day." Having our own way .generally means that we think ourselves a good deal wiser than those who wouldguide us. The result is often what happened to the captain of the good ship Central America. His vessel had sprung a leak, and showed signs of sinking fast. Signals of dis- tress were hoisted, and, to the joy of all, a ship soon approached. "What's amiss ?" cried the captain through his speaking trumpet. "We are in bad repair, and going down," returned the captain of the Central America. "Lie by till mornino." "Let me take your passengers on board," returned' the stranger. "Lie by till morn- ing," was the only reply. - When morning came, the Central America was gone, and all on board had perished. THE TRUE GENTLEMAN.—It is HO very uncommon thing in the world to meet with, men of probity ; there are likewise many men of honour to be found. Men of courage, men of sense, and men of letters are frequent; but a true gentleman is what one seldom sees. He is properly a compound of the various good qualities that embellish mankind. As the great poet animates all the different parts of learning by the force of his genius, an& irradiates all the compass of his knowledge by the lustre and brightness of his imagination, so all the great and solid perfections of life appear in the finished gentleman, with a beautiful gloss and varnish; every- thing he says or does is accompanied with a manner, or rather a charm, that draws the admiration and good- will of every beholder. WHITE ANT His.—ln ;India these ant-heaps seldom attain a height of more than a couple of feet, but in Cen- tral Africa they form veritable hills, and contain many tons of earth. The brick houses of the Scotch mission- station on Lake Nyassa haVe all been built out of a sin- gle ants' nest, and the quarry from which the material has been derived forms a pit beside the settlement some dozen feet in depth. A supply of bricks as large again could probably still be taken from this convenient depot, and the missionaries on Lake 'Tanganyika and onwards to Victoria Nyanza have been similarly indebted to the 1 sbours of the termites_ In South Africa the Zulus and Krsfars pave all their' huts with white-ant earth; and during the Boer war our troops in Praetoria, by scooping out the interior from the smaller beehive-shaped ant- heaps, and coverincr the -top with clay, constantly used them as ovens. A MERRY ri—" Good Wards " for May. EART.—Let us not distrust gaiety. The " heal, light heart" is a splendid gift of God. 'A merry heart is a continual feast." Innocent fun at home should not merely be tolerated, it should be planned for. Some houses settle down into a round of sober and re- spectable dulness, which drives young people out of them in search of diversion, and which is pleasing neither to God nor man. The Father who has made the earth so beautiful, filling it with colour, bloom, and song, has put no premium on acerbity and mere solemnity. He chides our thankless moods, and bids us rejoice ever- more. And most of us, thoughdlike the Psalmist, we may have said in our haste, "I am cut off from before thine eyes," yet when we sit down to make Up our ac- count with God, the acknowledgment must be, "Blessed be the Lord, for He bath shown me His marvellous kind- ness in a strong city. —Christian Union. Johnson tells us that "A man should keep his friend- ship in constant repair," Yes. It is true. "Now abideth Faith, Hope, Charity, these three; but the greatest of these is CharityP4• - What one does 'easily is apt to be his forte; though years may pass before he finds this out.—E. C. Stedhutn • Joy is never sown upon earth but in a furrow tfaced ,by labour and sorrow. You who seek joy-begin to en- dure and to labour.—" Golden Sands." \ Be thou *hat thou singly art, and personate only thy- self. Swim smoothly in the stream of thy nature, and live but one man.--.§ir Thomas Brown. . Grief speaks a common language and doth wring The heart of peasant as of mightiest king; Both are but men beside an open grave.--Fraser. Be humble, patient,-self-sustaining ; hope only for Oc- casional aids; love others, but not engrossingly, for by being much alone your appointed task can best be done! —Margeret Fuller. "No language,", to borrow the words of Chopin, "can express the power, beauty, heroism, and majesty of a mother's love. It shrinks not where man cowers, and grows stronger where man faints; and over the wastes of worldly fortune sends the radiance of its quenchless fidelity like a star in heaven." A lady—a French lady—is showing a visitor the family portraits in the picture gallery. "That officer i there, n the uniform," she says, "was my great great grandfather. He was as brave as a lion, but one of the most unfortunate of men—he never fought a battle in which he did not have an arm or leg carried away. Then," she adds, proudly, "he took part in twenty-four engagements." BEAUTY EVERYWHERE.—The remotest corner of the globe is full of wonder and beauty. The laziest bank in the world, away from towns, where no artists do con- gregate, upon which no farm laps, where no vines hang their cooling clusters, nor flowers spring, nor grass Invites the browsing herd, is yet spatted and patched with moss of such exquisite beauty that the painter, who in all his life should produce one such thing, would be a master in art and immortal in fame, and it has the hair of ten thousand reeds combed over its brow, and its shining sand and insect tribes might win the student's lifetime. God's least thought is more prolific than man's greatest abundance.—Henry Ward Beecher. ANECDOTES OF GREAT PREACHERS.—In an article on "The Antiquity of Jests," in Longman's Magazine for February, the writer, Brander Matthews, points out how frequently the parentage of jests is shifted from shoulder to shoulder. There is a story which ascribes an utter- ance, scarcely fit for ears polite, made on entering the pulpit on a sultry summer morning by a popular preacher, to Mr. Spurgeon in this country, and to Mr. Ward Beecher across the Atlantic. Strangely enough, an absolute denial to the assertion that these gentlemen were the authors of the jest, has been given by the friends of both•the well- )(flown preachers, and Brander Matthews discovers that precisely the same ill-favoured sentence was attributed to Rowland Hill and Robert Hall. '6 Who the real origi- nator was will not," he remarks, "be known with cer- tainty until the 'Authentic Jest Book' appears. 4 AN AWKWARD Mrseaxr.—At a recent Sunday School anniversary meeting, one of the speakers related the following anecdote on the consequences of "cramming" young heads with more than they can conveniently carry :—The Bishop of a certain diocese was to visit one of the parishes under his direction, and to stay for a night with the Vicar, so that there *light be no difficulty as to his reaching the church next morning in time for the confirmation service. The Vicar's page-boy had been instructed some time previously as to a special duty which would devolve upon him, viz., that of calling the Bishop in the morning. He was to knock at the door, when the Bishop would probably ask, "Who's there? In reply he had been told to say, 'lt's the boy, my lord ;" and, that there might be no mistake, the necessity, of perfectly learning his lesson was impressed upon him. Consequently at every convenient opportunity he re- peated it to himself over and over again. At length the eventful morning arrived, and, brimful of the importance of his duty, he knocked at the Bishop's bed-room door. As had been anticipated, the Bishop's response was, "Who's there?" But-alas for the boy, and alas for the teaching, the reply that came so promptly was—" it's the lord, my boy !" Mrs. Stowe gives a characteristic account of a gram- matical exercise at which her brother, Henry Ward, as- sisted in his school days. Young Beecher was about eleven years old, and as full as possible of fun and mis- chief. The teacher was drilling her pupils in the rudi- ments. "Now," Henry," said she, " 'a' is the indefinites you see, a_nd must be used only with the , singular dum- ber. You can say 'a man,' but you can't say 'a men," can you ?" "Yes. I can say 'a men,' too," was the rejoin- der. "Father always says it at the end of his prayers." "Come, Henry, don't be joking. Decline 'he." "Nomi- native 'he,' possessive 'his,' objective' hull.'" "You sea, 'his' is possessive. Now, you can say 'his book, but you cannot 'him book.'" "Yes, Ido say 'hymn book,' too," said the impracticable pupil, *ith a quizzical twinkle. ga,ch one of these sallies made his young teacher laugh, which was the victory he wanted. 'But now, Henry, seriously, just attend to the active and passive verbs. Now, 'I strike' is active ,you see, because if you strike you do something. But 'I am struck' is passive, because, if you are struck you don't do any- thing, do you ?" "Yes, I do—l strike back again." After about six months, Henry was returned on his ' parents' hands with the reputation of being an, inveterate joker and indifferent. scholar. , JOSEPH JOHNSON MILES.—In the course .of a short biography of this philanthropist, in Slotday Magazine, Hesba Stretton says :—There was one form of benevolence , which I think he must have originated, for I know of no other person who does the same kindness. Many years , ago he lost a son, seventeen years of age, who fell over the cliffs at Freshwater, in the Isle of Wight. He had insured this boy's life, only three years before, in the London Life Association, for £3,000,, The interest of this money, with his fee as director of the associaticn, he set aside to aid young men, especially clerks with , , families, to insure their lives, paying half of the annual premium for the first seven years, after which the pay- ment becomes a mere trifle. The sums insured were • from tlOO to £1,000; and the young men he thus helped amounted to hundreds. Many of them did not know who was thus befriending them; even I was not per- mitted more than a glance at the long list of names. I have known him visit a poor foreign governess in a hospital of whom he knew nothing but that she was poor and a stranger. He has picked up a workman whose Riot was crushed in the streets, taken him to St. Bartholomew's, and maintained his family until leis re- covery. Though rarely quitting London for pleasure he went to Lancaster, ostensibly to visit an old friend, but chiefly to see a little child in the Royal Albert Asylum there. The almshouses for poor booksellers, called the Booksellers' Provident Retreat, were a favourite resort to him; and this touching, pathetic note was written by one of the inmates shortly after his death :—" From my sick-bed I uplift my heart to God, that the name of the late Joseph Johnson Miles may be had in everlasting remembrance." Boys at school were affectionately re- membered by him; boys of all classes, and at all lands of schools. Young men found in him a friend always ready to advise and help them. He practically realised St. James's description: "Pure religion and undefiled &fore God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows irr their affliction, and to keep himself un- spotted from the world." This man living all his life in the heart of London, made it a life of simple goodness. THOMAS Fsen's EARLY YEARS.—For three hundred years the name of Feed, one of the rarest of Scotch sur- names, can be traced in Dumfriesshire. It is derived from the Scandinavian, and signifies a prophet or for- tune-teller. About sixty years ago the family was divided into the rich and the poor Feeds, and from the - latter branch the Subject of this article is descended. Thomas Faed was born on the Bth of June, 1826, at Bur- ley Mill, near Gatehouse of Fleet, in the Stewartry of Kirkcudbright, a district far removed from the turmoil of cities, and one in which primitive manners have lingered longer than in any other part of the Lowlands of Scotland. His father was the tenant of Burley Mill, and was not a miller, but a builder of mills. His know- ledge of machinery and its mysterious Ways was pro- , found, and he had a genius for invention; not, as a rule, a profitable kind of genius to its possessor. The result was that all his life he was somewhat of a disappointed , man. There was an artistic bent in the whole Burley' Mill family. Tom, influenced perhaps by the example and precept of his elder brother John, now a member of the Scottish Academy, began when very young to draw and to copy other people's drawings. Two bulky volumes in the Burley Mill_ library, entitled "The Bio- graphy of the Bible," illustrated with outline en- gjnyings from designs by Michael Angelo, Raphael, Sze., were a never-failing source of, wonder and delight to the young Feeds. On the walls of their aunt's parlour hung some drawings, which appeared to the eyes of the youthful students to be veritable masterpieces. Once upon a time an uncle of theirs had set off to England to push his fortune, and had returned without the fortune, but with a few oki- fashioned engravings, such as "Cupid Subduing the Tiger," "Louis in Prison," and others of a like nature.. These the uncle had copied in Indian ink, and the copies' were given to Faed's aunt. It was in recopying the &pies that the Faedi made their first essays in art. Tom Feed also followed out, in his own way, healthier methods of self-education, such methods as a born painter alwthys discovers for himself. In the picturesque scenery of the Stewartry he found congenial subjects for his pencil. Wandering by the banks of Burley Burn, and among the hills and lakes and messes of the district, and studying the rustic life with which he was sur- rounded, he laid the foundation of those tastes and sym- pathies that in later years have helped him to his most satisfactory triumphs. In summer time, when there was no grain to prepare, he used the old kiln-house as a • studio, and there, with a fair top-light and a background filled with Rembrandtesque shadows, he had, as sitters, nearly-, all the ragged urchins of the country side. In the meantime John Faed had settled in Edinburgh as a painter, and by his advice Thomh, in 1842, at the age of sixteen, began his regular art studies in that city.— Gar/ Words for May. n ANGELS' CAKES (Patented). NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HORTI- SULTURE,

Missrs.Geose Leigh ,and• Co., who have been 'very suctessful in importing and breeding Herefords in the United States, have fitted up a large breeding establish- ment near Aurora, 111., and stocked it with a selection from the best herds of England, including the champion bull Archibald (6290), who is doing excellent service in the herd, and his calves have sold from £2OO to £250 each. The cuckoo was heard on Sunday and Monday near Walton-le-Dale. The kingfishers have re-appeared in the district. The Brea is one of the moat favourite haunts for this handsome bird in North Lancashire, and we hear that several birds have in past years built their nests on the line of this pretty steam and got their young away in safety. , A HOG THAT WAS LOADED.—A despatch from Raleigh to the New York Tribune says :—The Enterprise, a news- paper published at Larinburg, in this State, vouches for the following A hog ate heavily of dynamite, and then entered a lot where there was a drove of mules, The hog Was kicked by one Of their number and Mime- diatelysexploded and killed twenty of the mules.": Mr. John Rowley, jun., of Norton, Doncaster, has sold his celebrated show bull, Self Esteem 2nd, to Mr. Hand- ley, Green Head, Milnthorpe,, for service.. Self Eateem 2nd won champion prizes at the Royal at York, also first at Shrewsbury Royal last year. Seft Esteem 2nd is a grandson of the celebrated Royal champion shorthorn prize-winner, Sir Arthur Ingram. - The E,arL,Of Spencer's entire herd of shorthorns at Althorp, forty-nine lots, with ten young cart horses, have been: disposed of by Mr. John Thornton. Althorn has an historical connection with sl orthorns extending from the• beginning of the present century. At the sale of Mr. R. Colling's herd in 1818 three cows and heifers and the bull Regent (544) were purchased, and sixteen cows and heifers were afterwards bought at Mr. Mason's sale at Chilton, 1829. THE REDUCTION OF RENT MOVEMENT.—A correspondent writes :—"LoreLonsdale and Lord Hothfield, two of the largest landowners in Westmorland, have recently been petitioned by their tenants for a reduction of rent The fact is more significant than will appear at first sight to those unacquaitted with, the economic and social conditions of the county, but no more emphatic evidence of the gravity and extent of the present crisis in agriculture could be furnished. Agricultural credit is higher in Westmorland than in most English counties, and the farmers of the county enjoy the deserved repu- tation of being among the most prosperous, contented, and thrifty of their class. The county has been among the last to suffer from the full effects of the adverse in- fluences which have brought about the prevalent pros- tration, and this result is largely due to two facts. In the first place, Westmorland is in the main a grazing county, and it has enjoyed a remarkable immunity from the foot-and-mouth disease; and, in the next place, the sturdy spirit and the.practical and vigorous instincts of the old race of yeomen still survive. It was asserted some time ago that the English yeoman was an extinct social type, but he continues to flourish in Westmorland and Cumberland. He is still a familiar figure in the sequestered dales of these two counties, and may be seen almost daily looking after his sheep on the bleak fells ; while on market day in most.of the small towns the russet-coated dalesmen,' owner and cultivator, may be seen in picturesque groups in the neighbourhood of the place that does duty for a corn market. Vacant farms in Westmorland are the exception, not the rule, and although low prices have seriously affected the in- come both of the arable and of the stock and dairy farmer, the tenants as a body have had less to complain of than agriculturists in other parts of the kingdom, But the depression is now so sorely felt that most of the farmers are crying out for redused rents. Lord IRAK- field replies that he will consider any case on its indi- vidual merits, but he declines to grant any general re- duction of rents." AGRICULTURE IN NORTH LANCASHIRE.—"R." writes : All vegetation appears to be waiting, and when the long- looked-for showers come, with heat, there will doubtless be a glorious burst of deferred growth. Oats, barley, potatoes, and carrots are in, and the land is being fast got ready' for mangOlds, cabbage, and swedes. We hope to complete marigold sowing this week. Stocks of pro- vender are, getting small, for although young cattle are let out for a few hours in the middle of the day, the pastures are so bare that there is little saving in fodder. Ewes and lambs are now on last year's seeds, or what there is of them, but there is evidently a scarcity of milk, for although-the lambs are healthy enough they do not make quick growth. Those who have silos are congra- tulating themselves, for one of my neighbours holds that the keep of stoclr from grass in silo and grass in hay fa as 15 cattle to 10. •Poultry-keeping, like everything else, can evidently be overdone. When in Westmorland, last week, I was struck with the number ai hen cotes scat- tered around the town of Kirkby Lonsdale. In almost every wood and field you came upon them, and in one field of about two acres there were from 100 to 200 fowls of various breeds. I was told that a craze had sprung up amongst the tradesmen and inhabitants for poultry keeping, owing to reading in the papers the profits that would resultirom such. , Naturally I inquired the price of eggs, and found that in the first week in April, with east winds prevailing and night frosts—certainly not the best time for hens being in full laying profit—that eggs were a complete drug in the market, and that the grocers were selling them out of the shops at 16 for is. I veri- fied thi9 by purchasing a box. Not much profit, here. I am afraid, for the producers. Milk fever in cattle has usually been considered, in this district, a preventable complaint, andmost of the Yorkshire cattle dealers think so little of it that they have no hesitation in buying cows that have suffered from it. It is considered to occur only in cattle kept in too high condition prior to calv- ing, and that if in-calf cattle are allowed .troper exer- cise, kept in ordinary store state, and given a few warm bran mashes and doses of linseed-oil a few days before calving, there need be no fear of milk fever. DISTRICT AGRICULTURAL NOTES.—A correspondent writes :—," In the course of the next few days, should weather such as we have now continue, we may expect to see a great area of oats " ebreward." The greatest portion of the oat seeding is finished, -end most of the land has been rolled to a surface of rare .fineness. In the north Wyre district oat sowing is more backward, as the farmers there prefer that when the young blades shoot.throug,h the earth there should be heat enough, to force the growth forward-at once. In their experience the, matter of a fortnight later at harvest time is prefer- able to the risks attending the delicate period of " spoan- ing." Nothing could surpass the condition of the ground in which oats have been sown. Wheat has grown rapidly within the past week, and is fresh and rich in colour, and in most cases the ground is quite covered ' with it. Of spring wheat we have less this season than for many years past. The work of planting potatoes has made very rapid progress during the week. Every effort has been strained to make the best of the weather and -the splendid condition of the land, and that effort has been well rewarded. The condition of the land is very fine. At the present I estimate that about two- thirds of the-area proposed to be devoted to the tuber has already been planted. This indicates an earlier lift- ing time of store potatoes than usual, which will render I the crop less liable to the ravages of the disease. The potato crop this year seems to demand more than usual attention—l refer to Lancashire and Cheshire specially, —for in the first place an unusually large area is being planted. I know one Lancashire farmer who is putting in 400 tons of store potatoes. The magnum is the favourite seed all round, and if the. season should be a favourable one for this variety we shall have an extra- ordinary yield. A great many young and dry cattle are out, but there is nothing to turn milking stock to for a few hours a day. Artificial grasses have freshened much during the last four days. What is wanted is warmth and rain. More grass in the pastures is abso- lutely required for the heavy stock of lambs which halt fallen, also for cattle. The milk dealers have begun to lower their retail nrices some of them have even re- duced to 3d. a quart." CHESTER FARSIERS' CLUB AHD CHEESEHAKIHIL--On Saturday afternoon, a meeting of the Chester Farmers' Club was held at the Blossoms Hotel, Chester, for the purpose of hearing a paper read by Mr. M. Hulse, of Tilston Hall, near Tarporley, on the subject of " Cheese- making." Mr. J. Podmore presided, and there was a fair attendance of members present.—Mr. Hulse, in the course of his paper, said that for the sale of stock they ought to have established live and dead weight, because it seemed a monstrous foolish thing that a farmer who had had all the expense and trouble of feeding stock change e chh oaounnlgdde smi shoe nal tt htt leei re weight them ee gwyhi tsthhoeef d lump instead of weight. The to cheese.ir direct e atthtoeuntgihotn tthoexwas u .the t to come to a firm stand, and only sell the 1121b5., which was the standard weight by Act of Parliament, instead of the 1211b5., which the factors now took, and, as they all knew, the one pound was not paid for. When he told them that the- one pound on the make of cheese in Cheshire, at-6d. per lb., amounted to £4,500 per year, he thought they would agree With him in saying there needed an alteration. (Hear, hear.) Thirdly, there was the question of labour. It had been frequently stated of late that the make of good, fine Cheshire cheese had gone back,- but he ventured to contradict that state- ment, and would aver that in Cheshire to-day the finest cheese in the world was made. On the other hand, they , knew that in the country some very inferior cheese was produced, and it was that inferior cheese they wanted to improve. The loss sustained by the production of inferior cheese was very serious and amounted in many instances to as much as 40s. the 1001 b. Before the cattle plague the make of cheese in the county was estimated at 11,000 tons, and it was probable that the make of Cheshire cheese might now be reduced to 9,000 tons. HO said if cheese could be made in Cheshire of such quality that it would realise 70s. per cwt., on the aver- age the return would be £630,000; but it was believed that the average in Cheshire was not more than 50s. per cwt., showing a loss of money to the producers Of £lBO,OOO. This item alone ought to be enough to stir up makers of inferior cheese to improve. If nsore of the farmers' wives nould take lessons, it would go to reduce the £lBO,OOO now lost in the county by the making of inferior chsese.—A discussion ensued.

THE LAST PRESTON CHEESE FAIR AS OTHERS SAW IT. —ln the course of an article in the last issue of the Agri- cultural Gazette, headed "A Peep at Proud Preston. The Royal Show Ground: A Cheese Fair," the -writer, after describing the Moor Park site, says:—"As I was return-

ing from the show ground I stepped off the tram when it reached what is dignified by the name of the "covered ,market" to have a lea at it; it is simply a monster shed ,coliering-an open area which formerly Went by the name of " Orldwick's Orchard." What was ray surprise, on walking to the western end of the shed, to find a cheese fair was being held: And oh, shades of Voelcker and Joseph,Harding, and of: our Professor Sheldon;what a sorry sample did I see! Oh for some one from the Duke of Westminster's Cheshire cheese factories, or for my I little friend Daiuton, who used to be at Budworth, and may• be there still, or for any one who knows how to handle milk and make it into what deserves to be called cheese—to come to teach these Lancashire cheese-makers how to do it! I wonder if land is low-rented in North Lancashire; it would need to be, or the makers of some of the cheese I saw will be in a fair way to bankruptcy. Fancy cheese made from rich milk selling, as I was told some lots did, att2os. per cwt.! That really represents .milk sold at less than 2d. per gallon, while I am told that the "kitting" farmers who deliver milk right from the farm to the consumer get in the summer Is. per gallon and winter is. 2d., and manage to do a bit of skimming into the bargain. It must not be misunderstood as to prices; they were very various, but, from what I could learn from the sellers, as a rule very unsatis- .factory ; and the wind-up of the affair was certainly sickening, for out of about 50 dairies nearly. 20 had to be carted home unsold. I heard of a choice lot which fetched 70s. which proves that people were present who ' would give a price provided they got the right sort of stuff. But how is it that the lower qualities are so many and the better so very very few? Certainly the latter makes of these Lancashire cheeses were the most pasty sort I have ever seen, and the older sorts had such a 'gassy' flavour—it is a peculiarly sickly flavour, and unlike what you meet with in, any other county.. Talking to an intelligent man, who evidently had no cheese at the' fair, but who seemed well pested up in cheese-making matters, he threw great blame on the way many farms were fitted up—telling me of large families crowded into such little space as really to be a condition disreputable to the owners. He said he could take me to a farm where', ten persons lived and a dairy of cheese was made, and only two small rooms on the ground floor, with two over them—no milk-house and no conveniencd for household work. Another complaint he made was of the bad sanitary surroundings at many dairy farms. Altogether he gave me a dark picture of the way dairy farms were fitted up in what is called 'The Fylde' district. If what he told me was not over- stated—and I see no reason why he should have exag- gerated to a strange enquirer like myself—there is little wonder why so very many bad cheeses are made. Of Course, I could not get much information at such a hasty visit, but what I did served to remind me of what I read recently, in your valuable, paper to this effect— that out of the more than a million last year lost by producing bad cheese from rich milk, that (roughly 'estimated) one-half the amount might be set down to the shortcomings of landlords in neglecting to provide suitable premises for their tenants, and the other half of the loss to want of skill on the part of the makers."

MR. BIGGAR, M.P.. AT WARRINGTON. - , THE POLICE AND THE NATIONALISTS. - ' On Sunday afternoonea meeting was held in-the Catholic Association Hall, under the auspices of the local branch of the Irish National League, for the purpose of hearing an address from Mr: J. G. Biggar, M.P. The subject of the address was" The duties of Irishmen, and Ireland's right to legislative independence." Mr. F. Loughlin, president of the local branch of the League, occupied-the chair, and there were, amongst ethers, on the platform Dr. O'Keeffe (Widnes), Mr. P. McKinley (St. Helens), Mr. Hughes, and Mr. Donoghue. There was a crowded attendance. The CuanywArr, who was received with cheers, mentiened that he had received letters of plogy for absence from I Mr. J. Denvir and Mr. P. Byrne (Liverpool), also two letters from Catholic clergy of Warrington—(applause)—who had I been invited to be present by the committee. But an they were aware, and as the letters stated, that was just the time of day when the clergy were engaged in their religieus duties, but they concluded their letters by wishing them every success and prosperity. (Applause.) He went on to say that the League, under the auspices of which that . meeting was being held, was a perfectly constitutional and legal organisation, for proof of which he pointed to the - fact that a branch existed in all the manufacturing centres of England in which Irishmen were in any great numbers. , If it had not been a legal organisation these would not have been allowed to exist for any length of time. There might be some in that meeting who held the opinion that that organi- sation was not so legal as he said it was, and he did not quarrel with those people for nit opinion, provided they - did not try to coerce kim to think as they thought. That brought him to the subject he wished to speak about. They were aware that branch had been in existence for about 12 months, and until very recently they had had no one to interrupt and molest them, but this last six weeks or two months the police had begun to pay them visits. He had no objection to that, but they went a deal further, for when their friends came from Liverpool or Manchester, or whet- aver they came from, the police thought it their duty to go down to meet them at the station. Well, they hadn't even any objection to that kind of thing. but wbat he did object I to was that they should act as they acted on the previous Sunday. They announced a committee meeting to be held on that day, but there was no announcement of a public meeting, nor in any sense was it to be a public meeting. It was to make arrangements for that meeting. But, as was known to many of them, the police came in, and on their respectfully requesting them to retire—he supposed feeling the strength of their power and the power of the law behind them—they refused to leave. (Mr. McKinley : " The Rus- sians have done the same," and loud applause and laugh- ter.) He thought the action of the police very unconstitu- tional, and a resolution was moved and carried that they retire but they had got in and they would not retire. The meeting was thereupon broken up, as they did not feel dis- posed to go on. They then naturally thought the matter would come to a climax, as they must either do one thing or the other. Either they must break up altogether or they ' must see whether the authorities sanctioned that kind of thing. He consequently went to the chief constable, who received him most courteously, and after the circumstances of the case had been laid before him, he promised him (the chairman) that as the police were obnoxious to them they should not trouble them any more. (Hear, hear.) Those were the chief constable's words, and he (the chairman) thought he had gained a great deal. He might say that the chief constable treated him to a great many, of his own political opinions—(laughter)-.and he (the chairman) told' him he was entitled to hold those °Onions in the same way that he was entitled to held his. (Hear, hear, and iaughter.) But little did he think 'when he left the chief constable . that almost before the ink was dry on the treaty, that gentleman would go and in another,way seek to break up that which he was not able to prove unconstitutional. (Hear, hear.) Many of them were aware to what he now alluded. The ehief, constable left the path of duty and followed his own private opinions, and with the power he knew to be at his back, he went to the different employers of labour—or caused others to do so—in•this town in order to put coercion in force against the men who would dare to belong te that ergan• isation or in fact even to be present at their meeting that day. (" Shame.") He (the Chairman) made that statement well knowing the responsibility that attached to him in the presence of the representatives of the prese—(hear, hear)— aud at the proper time and place if needs be he would prove what he now staled. (Applause.) But he was proud to say for the honour of Warrington and for the honour of the great employers of labour in this town, few listened to it. (Applause.) They no doubt had heard-the same tale before and would give no willing ear to it. Ile was very sorry to say that that was not unanimous, and that in some instances and notably in one—he would give no names—the manager was induced to fall into tha trap which he (the Chairman) considtered had been laid for him, and commenced in a mild way to interrogate the men whose names bad been previously given to him by the chief constable. Ha interrogated these men as to the part they had been taking in the organisa- tion and what part they intended to take. He (the chaix- man) would not s ty that threats of dismissal were held out, ut It was coming very near to coercion in his mind—(Mr. McKieley : "He will get French's dose yet" and laugh- ter ) Re thought that the individual to whom he referred had by this time regretted his conduct which had gone abroad. (Hear, hear.) Lie (the chairman) thought that at the time it would hardly be credited that a poor Irish work- ing-man would not only have to give his -labour for paltry wages, but also to throw in his politic,l opinions to the bargain. He supposed if that were carried on the work- ' min would next be asked to throw in his religious opinions. (Hear, hear.) He took it that their chief constable would next be establishing a registry office at the bridewell where employers might get to know—not the ability of Irishmen te do their work—tept their character and the colour o their politics. (Hear, hear.)* He as a ratepayer in Warrington for a great number of years, proteeted against the chief con- stable or anyone else dictating to On the colour of his poli- tics. (Applause.) c oercion had always hitherto failed'and he could premise the Irishmen of,Warriagton that it would be a failure in this 'case also, if they would carry ,on their meet- inga in the quiet constitutional manner they bad hitherto done. (1!...0nd applause.) • . Mr. DONOGHUE moved the following tesolution :—" That this meeting begs to record its unabated confidence in the Irish Parliamentary party, under the leadership of Charles Stewart Parnell, and pledges itself to do everything in its power to forward the Irish national programme." , _ - Mr. B. HUGHES seoonded the resolution which was car- ried by acclamation. , Mr. BIGGAR, who was received with load applause, said they might think that the present Irish Parliamentary party had not drawn sufficient attention to that very great ques- tion of self-government for Ireland, but the excuse he should be disposed to make far that epparent want of attention was the practical nature of Mr. Parnell's mind. Mr. Parnell's idea of politics was to get from time to time substantial reforms, and prove, as he had proved to the Irish people, that reforms could be had by a powerful, deter- mined, and honest Parliamentary party. The result of the conduct of Mr. Parnell would undoubtedly be to give a very large increase of poirer to the Irish Perliamentary party after the next general election. If Mr. Parnell had not shown his practical ability in time past, there was very great reason to believe that the Irish people wonld have become discouraged, and not given so warm a !import as they had to their Parliamentary natty. The opinidfd had been proved to be correct by the result of a recent election that a very great number pf the non- CathoLo population of Ireland, who had hitherto abstained from supporting the Ebb Parliamentary party, would in the futuee give their aid to it. They, therefore, hoped and believed that at the next general election they would get support in districts where the national Irieh (so called) were not in a majority. Thus the eyes of the people of England would be opened to see the real state of affairs. Tney were told that they would always be out-voted by the two English political parties; , but people who argued in that way ought to know that the great guiding influence of the leaders of the two polilical parties was net the question of principle but of self-interest. (Hear, hear.) It was an undoubted fact that in a new Parliament, with a strong Irish party, before that Parliament had' lasted very long, they would get offers from one or both of the parties, and to such an extent as they had never had before; because if the Whigs had a majority of say 40, and the Irish repre- sentatives, numbering 80 or 85, were able to turn the ma- jority for the Whigs into a majority of 40 or 45 for the Tories, the practical result would be that the Tories would make such an offer to the Irish party as would induce them to give them their eupport. He thought they would agree with him that the policy which the Parnell party had pursued of keeping themselves entirely aloof from any continuous entanglement with one or other of the two English parties, had been one of the most beneficial nature to Ireland, and one which in the future was likely to bring advantages to the Irieh pebple. He used the words "continuous entanglement." It was true that the Irish Parliamentary patty had from time to time supported the Tory party, and on other occasions the present Government. Why? Simply because they found it for their own interest. (Laughter and cheers.) He was of opinion that euch a thing as politicil principle did not exist in England. What had the present Government dons? Declared in favour of popular, rights? It had passed the ctilture, thus preventing the expression of the voice of the minority in the House of Commons, and struck 1 a greater blow at-freedom of speech than perhaps had taken place for the last two hundred years. What had the present Government done further? It had attacked the .popular party in Egypt, and that in the meanest and most hypocriti- cal and dishonest way. And what had:teen the effect of , this? Probably it would prove the indirert means of mak- ing England lose India, because they had proved !bar in- competence as military men to put down a few unarmed savages. The Government could not succeed in the smallest military enterprises, and bow, then, were they going to face a great Power like Russia? Their position was this—they must either eat the leek or be ruined. He did not believe the Government would fight Russia, which would continue to ask greater and greater conditions, so that the final result • would probably be that India would be dismembered. Then if one country took India, another would want Canada, and a third the Cape of Good Hope, so that in the end probably England would be confined to the one island which was at present called Great Britain. (Laugh!er.) Their chairman had pointed out to them another of the meannesses of the English Government, viz., the coaduct of the police in the town of Warrington, which was simply on a par with their conduct generally. These people sent their detectives to watch their meetings. Well, the members of that society did not care how mach they

COTTAGE GARDENING

TIIRMIPS.—A few of these secured early are cit much more value than a greater number when the season is further advanced, and anyone having a friable Boil in a sunny aspect would find it a most profitable crop, as there ought to be a brisk demand for them like every- thing else extra early. The roots, moreover, only occupy the ground a few weeks. Hitherto, Early White Dutch and White Stone have been considered the earliest varie- ties, and are still largely sown. Early Purple Munich, which came under, our notice last year for the first time, is however, much .earlier. The roots are-not so large as thewzorts named, but they are•very beautiful. Like all other kinds that are sown early, it quickly-runs to seed, and on that account should be disposed of as soon as they are fit for use. We have sown our first crop broad- cast, and we mixed twice the quantity of radish seed with the turnips, so that we have two crops instead of one, and the radishes are fit for use long before the tur- nips require the space they occupy. Birds are always troublesome to Any seeds coming up at this season of the year, and by sowing in this way the same protection frena these visitors answers for both. The ground should be well trod previous to sowing, and afterwards raked so as to secure an even Surface, or the seeds:will be at different depths when they come to be covered. After the sowing is completed the bed should have a gentle beating with the back of the spade, and then covered over with sufficient soil to hide the radish seed. _ .

Ltrr-rocm—A small patch of these may now be sown with the view of planting out when large enough. This crop is invariably sown too thick, so that by the time they are a couple of inches long they are completely., spoiled. Every plant where it emerges through the soil should have an inch of clear space all round it, but in- stead of that we often see the space occupied by a dozen or more.plants struggling for existence. --To sow thick is a safe rule, but it must be followed by early thinning. THE FRONT GARDEN.—" The soil of my front garden is so poor that nothing seems to grow in it" is the reply we frequently receive when we venture to remark on the paucity of flowers they may contain. A barrow-load of manure or road scrapings would in many instances work wonders on the majority of plants. Those who collect any horse excrement that may be deposited in -front of their doors, and place it round , the their plants summer, and dig it in in winter, have invariably tome thriving plants in tleir gardens. • There are plants that are!. adapted for all kinds of soils and situations. We have lovers of the hot, dry, sandy soil, as well as of the cool and moist, clayey ones. There are shade-loving plants, as well as those that thrive in the full sunshine, so that no- one need be without a few'suitnble plants. Many gardens may be made gay during the summer for the small sum of one shilling, and the poorer the soil the more. likely the success. Twelve penny packets of flower seeds will be ample to sow 12 circular patches of ground one foot in diameter. Assuming the garden to be poor, we would recommend the following selection for trial.:—Nasturtiums, either tall or-dwarf, according to requirements. If the tall ones are chosen, they should be planted in a row, six inches distant, 'against the wall of the dwelling or the fence, as they would overgrowth° other plants if, permitted to ramble over the surface of the soil. The dwarf ones form clumps a foot or so in height, and five seeds will be ample for , one patch. Mignonette is sure to succeed, and a packet will be foutid to contain sufficient seed for two or thren:patches. Many fail with this redolent, because they allow the slugs to destroy it when it is scarcely above the soil, and they then blame the seeds. The other suitable sorts are African Marigolds, Nemophila (blue), Lupins, Gilia Tri- oolor, Collinsia Bicolor, /Clarkia Elegans, Candy Tuft, Calliopsis Bicolor, Aquilegia (Columbine), and Virginia Stock. Additional ones may be selected from the fol- lowing :—Wallflowers, Pansy, Double Chinese Pink, Malope Grandiflora, Godetias of sorts, Eschsocholtzia of sorts, Centaurea Cyances, Saponaria Calabrica, Sweet Rocket, Prince's Feather, Polyanthus, and Sweet Peas. THE Wnrnow.—Aphis, especially the green fly, increase rapidly at this season of the year, and if the underpart of the leaves is not frequently examined they will soon become . numerous, and some of the leaves will turn sickly. They are, moreover, much easier destroyed if measures are taken at the threshold of their existence. Tobacco smoke is a deadly enemy to all aphis of this description, and one pipeful would do for two or three fair-sized plants, providing a paper hood is made to cover the plant so as to effectually confine the smoke round it. A quarter of an ounce of tobacco placed in a rag, and soaked in a quart of boiling water, and, when cooled so that it may be handled, squeezed till all the juice is out of it, will also make an excellent insecticide. If in this a piece of soft soap the size of a walnut is dis- solved, it will also make an effectual abluent if the plants are dipped in, or held over a vessel and the mix- ture poured over them.

It is the same with ; if he is not virtuous, he is likely to become vicicaS. Garbed tells us that 'The rough angles of temper are rubbed down in the daily, hourly friction of common life," and that "Life is longer, greater, purer, nobler, 'be- yond cothparison, for all the sweet ties and loving words of home." "Refuse not," said Dean Alford's father to the Dean, "to gather the flowers, though they be but daisies an buttercups, with which it pleases God sometimes to streiv the path of life; but remember that perennial and thornless flowers bloom only In the Paradise above." - "Who is your family physician, George ?" "Doctor Smoothpain. ' " What ! Why do you employ that hare- brained creature?" "Oh, my wife once asked him if he could tell her,why she always had cold feet, and he told her they were so small they couldn't hold blood enough to keep them warm. Since that she won't have any other doctor." " Mr. Smith, you said you suspected the prisoner was a rogue the moment you saw him. Why did you suspectloin I 2!' " Becos 'e 'ired my rooms without beatin' down the price." "Is this a rule without many exceptions ?" "Hit's a rule vithout no hexceptions, yer vorship ; 'onest 1 men are halways stingy, and neversatisfied hunless they git a shilling's worth of anything for tenpence." An old man would not believe he could hear his wife talk a distance of fiVe miles by telephone. --His better half was in a country shop several miles away, where there was a telephone, and the sceptic was also in a place where there was a similar instrument, and on being told how to operate it he walked boldly up and shouted, "fob, Sarah !" At that instant lightning struck the telephone wire and knocked the man down, and as he scrambled to his feet he excitedly cried, "That's Sarah, every inch." div.p: watched, for they had nothing to conceal. He had said on DEARS' many platforms and in the House of Commons quite as L much as'ever he had said privately, and he dic not care if the .detectiyes watched him from one end of the world to the 11811EARS' Other. (Laughter.) They said before the world that they -"- hated England, and they did so as a political system They asserted before the world that they wanted Home Rule for IPORARS' Ireland, and they would have it if they could. (Cheers.) -4.1- ' They also said to them in Warrington that they wished ' that, if possible, they should act in that town as the mem-, "DEARS' bens of the Irish -party did in the House of Commons. Let; them in Warrington be quite as important and powerful rn their sphere as the members of the Irish Parliamentary p-- party were in theirs. In that borough they had the power to relegate to private life, a very obscure individual named 1 -1-.IEARs, Mr. McMinnies. (Laughter.) He supposed they would do '— so at the next election. He believed it would be the duty of the Irish party to ask their friends every- arsEARs, where to put out of office the Whip and put the Tories in a small majority. What they must do was simply this--what they believed to be for the good of the l "maw Irish cause. As to Mr. McMinnies, it was co honour at all 1— to be a member of Parliament of his type; and on the other hand it might be for the interest of the Irish people that a .IDEARS' rank Tory should be returned as the member for Warrington—one who would vote for measures favourable to Ireland if he thought it to his interest to do so. There 12111EABS' was not a single bit ,of difference between the two men. L. They both hated Ireland, and did all they could 'against it, unless they thought it was for their own interest, in par- ['DEARS' ticular cases, not to do so. The question of quality or A- merit between Mr. McMinnies and a Conservative was one of the smallest and of the least importance for them to con- [)EARS' eider. Let them remain perfectly free and unfettered until the proper time came, when a manifesto would be issued by Mr. Parnell in his own name, or after consultation with pEARS' other members of the party, calling upon their friends in Warrington and everywhere else to go in a particular direction at the general election. The policy of supporting pEARS' the Tories at the next general election was probably dictated by motives of a double nature. Firstly, they believed that la some of the agricultural counties the Whigs would re- place the Tories. In the next place the present Government, as represented by the present Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, had acted in so disreputable e. manner. Earl Spencer ha'd committed wilful murder; he had recognised sodomy; he bad committed all the crimes for which, if justice were done, be would be in the hands of the public executioner for some of them, and for others would be committed to penal servitude for the term of his natural life. (Laughter and cheers.) The speaker next urged the members of the society to adopt such measures as they thought best to make its meetings , attractive, and to hold them so frequently that they would, , by reason vf this, get rid of the abominable espianage insti- tuted by the Warrington detectives. (Cheers) Mr. Cox moved, and Mr. CONWAY seconded, a vote of thanks to Mr. Biggar, which was carried by loud acclama- tion.
Mr. Bromin, in responding, advised the Irish ratepayers of Warringtcm to endeavour to place representatives on local bad es. Re also moved a vote of thanks to the chair- man.
Mr. MAHONEY seconded this vote, which was cordlally carried, and briefly responded to by the CHAIRMAN. The meeting then ended.

div.head: MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.
div.p: THE MANAGEMENT OF POULTRY.

_ THE PREVENTION OF DISEASE. T. , • If all fowls could have unlimited runs, with good houses and natural food, there would be very little fear of disease. The benefit derived from a free use of the muscular powers is incalculable. By excercise every ' part of the body is strengthened, the organs are made to act freely, the blood to circulate regularly, and there il is thus laid up a supply of that reserve force which is so , necessary to all living things, and without which there is nothing to fall back upon in consequence of an unex- -1 pected strain upon the system. A fowl kept under these ' conditions is IoS6 likely to be attacked by disease for / when in a perfect state of health it presents vulner- able part. There must be a sympathy between disease , and the body it attacks, ere it can find an entrance thereto—sympathy in the form-of some weakness or enfeeblement. A healthy man can walk through &lever ward. He is like a strong embattled fortress. Disease is baffled by him. He throws it off like a duck the water from its back. But given a slight cold, a sluggish liver, an obese condition, and there is a break in the outer walls which disease Will assuredly find out. The man whose mode of life compels plenty of exercise, who lives in the open air, who is ever on the move, is less likely to be attacked by disease than is he whose habits are sedentary. The same thing applies equally to -fowls. ,We tried to show in our last article that food must be regulated by the conditions under which the fowls are kept, and that which is quite suitable for birds at liberty may be most injurious to those in confinement. The want of exercise can in this way be somewhat overcome. As the man of sedentary habits is worse than foolish if he attempts to eat the same heat-producing food as his neighbour who earns his bread "by the sweat of his , brow," which he will discover to his cost sootier or later, so it is that fowls fed upon rich foods; which may per- haps be given to -those in freedom, will soon develop di,sease in one form or another.. Food is the fuel, and the fuel should be given in accordance with the tax upon the machine. , But though there can be no doubt that fowls would be healthier if they had perfect freedom, this is not possible in every case. In the human species, necessity compels the crowding together of masses of the population, and the area which can be given to each one is thus very limited. And the same applies -to poultry. -The ques- tion, therefore, becomes a pressing one, Can this be over- come, and if so, in what way ? We have tried to show , how the evil effects of confinement can be obviated, as , far as that is possible; and now we must show how the best can be made of existing conditions in order to oc- ' oupy both the minds and bodies of the birds. Of course, 'on farms there need be no difficulty whatever. The space is there, and our advice is, utilise it Scatter your stock as widely apart as you can. They will do no harm whatever to growing crops, even though these be but a few in:ches above the ground. In France it has been found that poultry is the best protection against the deadly phylloxera, which have :been so destructive to the vineyards there. And many a crop of roots which have been attacked by insects would have been saved therefrom if a poultry-house had stood in one corner of the field, and the fowls been permitted to roam over it. When there. is the space, farmers need not have any trouble about exercise. Much can also be done `eien by those who are not so favoured, and a little ingenuity will koddevise means of giving occupation to the birds. Runs may be planned , to obtain the best results in this way.sf We think long narrow runs better than square ones, as:the birds are induced to cover much more ground in,: one than the other. They generally wander up and down by the side of one fence, and that dearest to the walks up which the attendant comes; and therefore, if the run be a long one, they will have a longer space to travel. Those who have not runs of this kind, but prefer to have small runs, with a Square in the centre or side, can make the best of this by forsaking the ordinary square that is so common. There is yet another class of poultry-keepers—namely, those who must have the birds in a-small run, perhaps not covering more than forty or fifty feet. t This class need to study the food question most of all. But by doing so, and making the birds work for their living, even they can succeed in maintaining the birds in health and profit. Belying the corn below a heap of earth or sand is a capital method, and this can be done regularly with very little trouble, when the heap is once provide& Hanging up every day a cabbage or turnip by string, and at such a ,height that the birds can just reach it, is also very useful in the giving of exercise. They will not fail to get much fun out of it, and the attempts to obtain it will, with the constant bobbing about of the vegetable, compel them to run about with it. We have also found it a good plan to give a cabbage leaf by leaf. If a large piece of any green vege- table—just as much as a fowl can carry, but more than'it can swallow—is thrown down, one will seize it, and the others will chase it around, trying to obtain part of the dainty morsel. A very large amount of exercise can be induced by a single cabbage in this way, if it is given in the way indicated. And exercise is ot so much importance that considerable trouble ought to be taken in order ta secure this to the fowls. They need to ,be encouraged, for a restriction of area induces indolence. The hints here given, will indicate those within reach of the poultry-keeper. With the lovely weather we have had, sitting hens will now begin to be troubled with fleas, unless some provision is made for keeping them down. These pests breed during the spring and summer in enormous num- bers, and often so irritate hens that they. desert their nests, besides being a great cause of gapes in the chicks. This may, in a large. measure, be prevented by providing a goad dust bath, in which plenty of carbolic powder is mixed. Hens can now be allowed off the nest for 20 or 30 thinutes so long as the weather keeps warm, and this will give them plepty of time to,dust themselves as well as feed. A plan we have heard highly spoken of is to saturate some of the rest straw with paraffin or petro- leum, taking care to keep some clean straw on the top. This will drive away insects, and do no harm to eggs or hen.

Orders were received at Sheerness, on Tuesday, directing the No. 4 torpedo boat to prepare immediately for active service. Thorneycroft, Chiswick, are building ay torpedo boats for the Government, and Messrs. White, of Cowes, another 20. Each boat is to be fitted with the latest im- provements, and will cost £ll,OOO. Alderman COTTON moved an amendment to Clause 4 with I a view of giving four members instead of two to the City of London.—Sir C. DUKE opposed the amendment, which was withdrawn Mr. IdEacy moved an amendment to Clause 9, with a view of excepting the county of Dublin and the counties in the province of Ulster from the Clause which deals with the division of counties.—Mr. TIZEVELYAN objected en be- half of the Government, to the amendment as involving a depirture from the principle on which the Bill was founded. —The amendment was withdrawn. in the branches (Engineer and Artillery) to which those whom he now addressed belonged. His Royal Highness concluded ty informing the cadets that those selected for the Royal Engineers would, after being commissioned, con- tinue their studies according to the usual system at Chat. ham, but that those selected for the Royal Artillery would not have this privilege. Being required for service, they would have six weeks leave, and would then be at once l .pomsteedettros.tih,ehiorrbnaetyteerroiEfsts workmen are engaged night and day upon 25 first-class torpedo boats recently ordered by the Government. Each boat is to be 125 ft. long and 1211. Sin. broad, with a maximum speed of 20 knots. They are built of steel, hive a draught of only 18 inches, with a speed of 16 knots, and it is understood that in the event of war with Russia they could be used for landing troops at any point which it was intended to storm. In the course of a few days these vessels will be ready for trial. An order was received at Portsmouth, on Wednesday, directing five more gunboats of the Comus class to be brought forward for commission. Acoordingly the Gadfly was launched on Wednesday afternoon. Tney will be all commissioned immediately. In view of being employed on active service, the Devastation, which is to be commissioned at Portsmouth, has been furnished with ten Nordenfeldts and four Gardner guns in addition to her original armament of four 35.t0n guns. The 2nd battery of the Ist brigade Southern Division Royal Artillery, stationed at Ports- mouth, on Wednesday received orders to embark at an early date for Singapore, to augment the garrison there. The Peninsular and Oriental Company's mail steamer Ravenna, 3,302 tons (Captain Stewart), left the Royal Albert Docks, London, on NVednesday, with 10 tons ord-

nance stores for Quetta. These stores include a carriage for a Gardner gun. She also takes out £60,000 in gold packed ia boxes for Satz, for the payment of the troops and other military demands. She also takes out a quantity of bar silver for strengthening the reserve of the banks in India.

div.p: THE REPORTED MEDIATION OF GERMANY.

BERLIN, T1711835AY. Reterrinz to the report that the Czar had expressed to the Emperor William an opinion that the prospects of peace were diminishing, the National Zeitung to-day positively fates that ne letter or telegram has lately been received by the Emperor William from the Czar. The journal adds :—The German Government observes a perfectly neutral attitude in the conflict between England and Russia, and that no inquiry concerning the disposition of Germany to undertake mediation has reached the Govern- ment either from Russia or England. THE SUEZ CANAL. To provide against the contingency of the Suez Canal be- coming blocked should war break out, the Government is despatching very large quantities of coals to the Cape for the use of the cruisers and other English war vessels. PROPOSED NEUTRAL LEAGUE.

An Exchange Company's telegram says the Paris papers are discussing a proposal that, in the event of a conflict be- tween England and Russia,the other European Powers should form a neutral league. The proposal has been entertained, though so far informally, by France. Germany, and Austria. Attempts are being made to induce Italy and Turkey to join the leogue, hut neither of those Powers has given a decided reply. Meanwhile, semi-official pourparlers continue on the subject. THE ATTITUDE OF DENMARK.

A Central News telegram, dated Copenhagen Wednesday, says :—The Danish Government has resolved to maintain a friendly neutrality. The army and navy are being strength- ened by call:ng out the reserves, and conscription is antici- pated. The sea forts are also being strengthened here. Sympathies are divided between England and Russia. It is stated that the Empress of Russia is earnestly advocating peace.
A COAL FAMINE IN ST. PETERS- BURG.

The State Line steamer Nebraska has been chartered by the Government for special service. The vessel, which is the best in the State Line fleet, goes round from tbe Clyde to Cardiff on Friday to ship a large quantity of coal. It is reported in business circles in Glasgow that in St. Peters- burg the scarcity of coal is so great that most manufac- tories will be compelled to cease operations unless the sup- plies can be replenished within a fortnight. It appears cer- tain, therefore, that a great many manufactories will be obliged to close altogether if war breaks out.
REPORTED ULTIMATUM OF RUSSIA.

ST. PETERSBURG, TIIESDAY.—A RllBBlBl2 ultimatum was it is said, sent on Sunday morning by a special official in the Ministry for Foreign affairs. The ultimatum calls up3n England for an immediate answer whether she ac- cepts the first boundary proposition of the Russian Govern- ment. If she does not accept that proposition the Russian troops will immediately receive orders to advance against Herat. The Emperor has ordered the mobilisation of all the Russi&nforceL—Dinly News..

div.head: 'TELEGRAM. FROM THE RUSSIAN GENERAL.
div.p: 'TELEGRAM. FROM THE RUSSIAN GENERAL.

ST. PETERSBURG, TIIIIRSDAY.—The Officiat 211essenger to•day publishes the following telegram from General Komaroff, despatched from Askabad last Friday.: —"The telegram prohibiting the occupation of Penj- deh reached me on March 23rd. As I only communi- catecilt to the commanders of the outposts, it was not ' generally known. Lieut.-Colonel Zacrszevski, with my permission, interviewed and corresponded with the British officers, but entirely in a private capacity. I did not admit that they had the right to carry on official pour parlert, and I adiressed my demands direct to the commander of the Afghan detachment. Colonel Alikhanoff, with a sotnia of Turkomans, rode in the direction of Morkela, along our bank of the river. To advance to Penjdeh was by no means my intention. To march in the daytime with a sotnia armed with sabres only, in the rear of a detachment four thousand strong, is inconceivable. One company marched on the heights on the right bank of the Murghab, but did not even reach cur vedettes on the left bank. When the Afghans began to approach the company returned by order to the camp. In view of the constant movements extend- ing over hundreds of verste it is not possible for me to fur- nish accurate periodical reports, but I shall report as far as possible anything worth noticing. Extraordinary inunda- tions of the rivers and water courses have interrupted com- munications. To cross the river ija only possible for accomplished swimmers. There was nothing new to report from Sarakhs up to the 18th inst. SIMLA, Truunsnev.—The reported occupation of Meru- chak by the Russians is regarded in official circles here as doubtful. It is expected that a British Military Mission would be sent to Teheran.
SIR PETER LUMSDEN AND GENERAL KOMAROFF. - RUSSIAN OFFICIAL
STATEMENT.

A Central News telegram, dated St. Petersburg, Thurs- day, says :—The following official statement has been issued to-day :—The official telegram from Sir Peter Lumsden, dated the 17th of April, attributing the combat on the Kushk River entirely to the aggressive action of General Komaroff in violating the Anglo-Russian Convention ,cannot yet be minutely refuted, the journey of the officer charged by General Komaroff with the delivery of his explanations being retarded by the bad state et the roads. The Govern- ment, are, however, in possession of sufficient information to prove the injustice of General Lumsden's suspicions. The Government were desirous of deciding the question of the frontier delimitation by friendly negotiation. According to the former stipulation the Russian Government consented to the delimitation by a special commission, but the unex- pected progressive movements of the Afghans on Penjdeh,the Murglaab, and the Hen i Rud obliged the Russians to take measures for the defence of their rights. Consequently, at the commencement of January, General Komaroff was in- structed to occupy a line drawn from Zulticar, on the Hari Rod, through Cekbrieilias, Ketbrissoume, Ischemenibia, and liousikan on to Put-I-Killed, terminating at the Old Bridge of Taschkepri. This lane formed a frontier west of the Penjdeh oasis, and the Ruasian. commanders received orders to abstain from conflict unless provoked by Afghan aggression. The localities above enumerated were occupied by the Russians on the 20th of February, and on the 4th of March the English Ambassador at St. Petersburg was informed of the fact, and stated that the Afghans had re- ceived orders not to attack the Russians, but to prevent their advance. He begged of the Russian Government to order General Komaroff not to advance. To this request the Russian Government consented, with all reserve, know- ing that Komaroff was at Taschkepri and the Afghans at Ak Tepe. The order was given that Penjdeh should not be occupied. The information furnished to the Russian Government corresponded with the facts announced to the English Government by Sir Peter Lumsden, who himself said that the Russians occupied Pul-i-Khisti and the Afghans Penjdeh. The English promises that the Afghans should not advance were thus falsified. The occapation of the right bank of the Kushk River occurred on the 251 h of March, on which day General Komaroff reached Taschkepri, and found the left bank of the Kushk Bay and Penjdeh oc- cupied by a handful of Afghans. In order to guarantee the safety of his detachment, General Komaroff demanded that the Afghan commander should immediately evacuate the left bank of the Kush's.. The refusal of the Afghans caused the fight of the 30th. Thus the statement of Lumsd.en that General Komaroff acted contrary to the convention as com- pletely unjust, for in exacting the evacuation of the left bank of the Kushk, Komaroff only fulfilled the orders he received, being unable to explain why the English officsrs Insisted that the facts were the contrary. The Government telegraphed to General Komaroff, and received in reply a telegraphic report from the General at Sarakhs, despatched on the 24th inst. [lle telegram from General Komaroff is given above.] THE REPORTED RUSSIAN ADVANCE. It was officially announced on Thursday, that there was no truth in the reported advance of the Russian troops to Maruchak. General Komaroff and Colonel Alikbanoff (ac- cording to the Pall Mall Gazette) were at Sarakhs on the 20th. and the detachment remained at Pul-i-Khisti.

div.head: PORT HAMILTON AND HERAT.
div.p: PORT HAMILTON AND HERAT.

MOSCOW, TAURSDAY.—The Moscow Gacette to-day de- clares that if England wishes to avoid war she must evacu- ate Port Hamilton, as otherwise Russia will be obliged to retort bv the occupation of Herat. The jpurnal further ex- presses its belief that the question of peace or war must now be settled within a few days.

div.head: OUR DEFENCELESS PORTS.
div.p: OUR DEFENCELESS PORTS.

At the annual meeting of the Renfreyrshire Commissioners of Supply, held at Renfrew on Thursday, Sir Archibald C. Campbell called attention to the fact that there was at pre- sent no guardship or gunboat in the Clyde, and that, with no torpedoes and no proper forts, an armed cruiser right without any difficulty attack G^eenock and destroy the shipping of the river. He suggested that they should ad- dress memorials on the subject to the Home and Foreign Offices. The suggestion was unanimously agreed to.

CURIOUS LETTER TO THE QUEEN.—At the present mo- ment, when the public mind has been educated concerning the River Cameroons, on the West Coast ef,Africt by the recent action of the Germans there, the following curious letter, addressed to Her Majesty the Queen, will be read with interest. It appears in the recently-publislnal corres- pondence respecting the aff sirs in the Cameroens, and will Show the desire the chiefs had of their country being under the British authorities :—Cameroons River, Acquab Town, August 7th, 1579. Dearest Madam,—We, your servants have join together, and thoughts its better to write ::ou a nice loving letter, which will tell you about all our wishes. We wish to have your laws in our town. We want to have every fashion altered ; also, we will do according to your Consul's word. Plenty wars here in our country. Plenty murders and plenty idol worsllippers. Perhaps these lines of our writing-will look to you as an idle tale. We have spaen to the English Consul plenty times about having an English Government here. We never 11 lye answer Irons you, so we wish to have acswer ourseves. When we heard-about Calabar river, how they have all English laws in their towns, and how they have put away all their superstitions, oh, we shall be very glad to be like Calauar now. Mris. S. A. A SECULARIST'S BEQUESTS.-A Bolton secularist, named Stephen Bulmer, a retired haedloo n weaver, has bequeathed £l,OOO to Mr Bradlaugh. He also leaves his dwelling to the local secular society, to be used as a secular hall. The deceased makes a provision of 128 a week for his wife. In the Queen's Bench Division, en Wednesday, Alica Maud Havgarth, widow, resi,ling at Maidenhead, sued William Goggs Bunting, of Little Marlow, Bucks, to re- cover damages for breach of promise of mar:iage. The action was not defended, and the plaintiff was awarded £450 damages. OUTBREAK OF SWINE FEVER IN CHESHIRE.—SWiIIe fever has broken out on the farm of Mr. Moss, Burleydam, Nara- wich. Two animals have died of the disease, and gne has been destroyed. There have been ten cases in other parts of the county during the week. Eight animals died, and two were immediately killed .and buried in quicklime.
