div.head: FORD.
div.p: FORD.

OTTAWA, SATURDAY.—Gene-rAI Middleton continued his march ts Batouche this morning. The Indian sharpshooters concealed in the bluffs caused many casualties. Two of General Middleton's aides-de-camp were wounded, and a bullet passed through the General's cap. According to in- telligence received here from Battleford, the loyal forces have scoured the whole of the Battle River Valley without seeing the Indians. The troops now on the way to Edmon- ton have re-established communication with that place. Couriers from Edmonton state that General Strange's march will be unopposed Deep anxiety continues to be felt con- cerning the fate of the men, women, and children who are held captive by Big Bear, at Fort Pitt. OTTAWA, SUNDAY.—News has been received from Prince Albert by a messenger who left there az Tuesday last, and who ran the gauntlet of Riel's forces, and swam the river, which is full of floating ice. The messenger states that there are 800 Indians at Prince Albert. The loyal forces have 500 rifle, but supplies are scanty, and the men are consequently on half rations. They are being constantly drilled, owing to a threatened attack by the Indians from the north district. Further details of the engagement at Fish Creek state that 25 rebels were counted dead upon the field. Itiei's chief lieutenant, Gabriel Dominant, is also reported to have been killed. Hie, who was himself present during the engagement, has gone to Batonahes to obtain reinforcements. General Middleton has decided to make the ravine his battle-ground with the rebels. Telegrams from Ottawa state that Riel is planning an attack on General Middleton's little force, and that a general uprising of the Indians Is anticipated. Fort Qu Appelle is in a perilous position, and the settlers in the vicinity of the fort are hastily arming. PANAMA.

PANAMA, SATIIIIDAY.—The United States troops occupied this city yesterday, and arrested General Aizparu, the rebel leader, together with the officers of his s'aff. The object of this is to preserve order. NEW YORE, MONDAY.—A telegram has been received here from Panama stating that the United States troops withdrew from the city on Saturday night, under the terms of an agreement concluded with General Aizpuru and the French Consul, by which the insurgent leader guarantees the maintenance of order. END OF THE INSURRECTION.

At the eleventh hour fighting has been averted in Pana- ma. General Aispurn has surrendered the town, and has withdrawn his troops. Panama is now occupied by the Colombian forces. All political offenders are to be pardoned, with the exception of those implicated in the burning and pillage of Colon. Further trouble is unexpected. SETTLEMENT OF THE FRENCH-EGYPTIAN

div.p: DISPUTE.

PARIS, TRES/Ult.—The Journal des Debate announces that the Bosphore Egyptien affair has been settled through the intermediary of England on the following bases :—The Egyptian Government will apologise to the French diplo- matic agent; the office of the Bosphore Eyyptien will be re-opened, and allowed to appear immediately. Canso, WRDNESDLY.—EogIand, France, and Egypt have come to the following arrangement on the Bosphere Ey yp- tien question :=Nubar Pasha will call upon the French dip- lomatic agent. The French demand for the punishment of the officials who executed the order for tke suppression of the Bosphore Eggptien is abandoned. The mode of execut- ing the press law in Egypt will be made the subject of im- mediate negotiations. The printing press and office of the Bosphore Eyyptien will be re-opened unconditionally. There is reason to believe, however, that the journal will not reap- pear for the present. FRANCO-CHINESE CONVENTION.

Pants, %YEW( ESDAY. - The Temps publishes advices from Toncinin to the effect that immediately after the arri- val of the Commissioners the Chinese force withdrew. The Chinese delegates at Tieostin have entered into courteens relations with the French delegates pending the arrival of instructions from their respective govern- ments.

div.p: SOUTH AFRICAN AFFAIRS.

CAPETOWN (VIA PLYMOUTH), APRIL B.—The Commis- sioners on the Boundary Line are now at work near Rooi Grond. Major Edwards has been despatched with a small party to treat with the native chiefs who wish to come under the protectorate. Gassitsiwe, in the course of several inter- views with Sir Charles Warren, has glyea full details of the depredations on his cattle, and of cruelties perpetrated OR his people bs Gay's volunteers, recruited from Stellaland and the Transvaal.

div.head: IRISH CATHOLIC BISHOPS IN ROME.
div.p: IRISH CATHOLIC BISHOPS IN ROME.

ROME, TUIIRSDAY.—The Irish Catholic bishops assembled this morning at the Propaganda, the proceedings being opened by an address from Cardinal Sitneoni. The bishops undertook to treat the questions submitted to them uninflu- enced by any political considerations. The Prefect of the Propaganda will give a banquet in their honour.

div.head: GENERIUJ NEWS.
div.p: GENERIUJ NEWS.

At a meeting of the Cabinet Council, on Tuesday, all the Ministers were present, including earl Spencer. John Purcell, labourer, surrendered himself to the police, on Tuesday, confessing be had murdered his mother, but failing to discover anything of the occurrence, they believe he is under a delusion. ManvELLous ESCAPE.—A girl has bad a marvellous escape from death near Stirling. She was walking on the railway when a train of six carriages knocked her down and passed over her without doing her the slightest injury. GRELT JEWELLERY TatFr.—At Dublin, on Thursday. Arthur Cole, a private in the 16th Lancers, was sentenced to six months' imprisostnent for stealing jewellery of the value of £2,000, the property of his master, Captain Craw- ford, of the 16th Lancers, whilst the latter was at Punch- town races. SECESSION OF 10,000 PEOPLE FELON WESLEYANISSL—In- formation from Tonga, South Seas, reports the SeCSSSiOn Of 10,000 people from the Wesleyan Church to the Free 'Church of Tongs. The ministers have seceded with the people, and it is thought the pastors initiated the step. In the Eurnber is included the European ministers, 12 native ministers, EiDO local preachers, 600 teachers, and 600 leaders.

LEE MURDER OF A POLICE INsPaoroa.—The trial at the Central Criminal Court, London, of Dav:d Dredge and James Lee for the marder of Inspector Simmons at Romford was concluded on Tuesday. The jury returned a verdict of guilty against Lee and not guilty against Dredg,.. Lee protested his innocence. Mr. Justice hawking, in passing sentence of death, expressed entire concurrence with the verdict.

AN IRISH RESIDENCE FOR P/INCE ALBERT VICTOR.—IC is said that it is is contemplation to parchasa Ardbroccan Palace, Nevan, as an Irish residence for Prince Albert Vic- tor. The place is capitally situated for hunting and salmon fishing, and has extensive stables and kennels. It is ex- plained that the trace Bishou of Meath will not ha able to keep up such an establishment, and that the palace will be soon for sale. ATTEMPT TO PorsoN A HUSBAND.—At one of the London police courts, on Monday, Charlotte Johnson, living at Wel- thamstow, was charged with causing poisonous drugs to be administered to her husband, who, during the last twelve months, has been living apart from her. The prosecutor's eon said his mother bad on several occasions given him powders, sometimes labelled "Poison." which he put in-hie father's tea at her instigation when his father was not look- ing. His father complained of being ill after taking the powders. Whilst the case was proceeding the prosecutor fell in a fit and was carried out of court. The prisoner was remanded until Saturday. A.M.C. OF THE MANCHESTER lIRITY.—The annual mov- able committee of the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows will be held this year at Aberystwith during Whit-week, May 25-30. On January let the Manchester Unity numbered 593,850 members, against 579,366 in 1834, showing a net increase of 14 484, of which 5.582 were in tbe colonies. The deaths numbered 7,078; 18,304 left the Ueity, and 3,000 are suspended. On account of the 7,078 deaths funeral benefits amounting to £73,551 were paid, and £26,124 on the death of 3,90/ members' wives, and £2,366 on the de- cease of former members' widows. There are in Lancashire 57,395 members, in Cheshire 16.816, Yorkshire 56,838, and in Derbyshire 17,049 members.

SERIOUS RIOT, ix LONDONDERRY THEATRE.-011 MOB. day night, in Londonderry Theatre, a riot °enured daring the performance ef a pantomime. In one of the scenes a number of portraits of public men were shown, the last ex- hibited being that of tits Prince of Wales. This was the signal for cheering and hooting. A large number of the audience called for cheers for Parnell and O'Brien, and a scene of great excitement prevailed. Air • attempt was made to continue the performance, but it was found impos- sible to da so. A portion of the audience commenced sing- ing " God save the Qaeen," and others "God save Ireland." Forms were thrown from the gallery into the pit, and the eudience rushed from the theatre in alarm. Further dis- turbance outside was prevented by the police. THE IMPORTATION OF FOREIGN CATTLB —At a meeting of working-men on Saturday, at Hackney, London, it was unanimously carried:—" That this meeting views with alarm the proposal of Mr. Chaplin, M.P , to prohibit the ex- clusive importation of cattle from Germany and other Con- tinental countrieeon the plea that the stocks and herds of England Buffer by foreign contagion of foot-and-mouth disease; whereas it is conclusively proved that foot-and- mouth disease, so much exaggerated by Protectionists for their own benefit, is indigenous to England, and not of for- eign origin."—A further resolution was carried :—" That this meeting impresses upon tbeir fellow working-men that all candidates for Parliamentary honours should be inter- viewed, and that no support should be given to them unless they give a promise to vote for tho repeal of the Acts, should they be returned."

ERIr, M.P., AND THE CRISIS.—Mr. John Bright, M.P., replying to the Society of Friends of Lancas- hire and Cheshire, urging the Government to submit the Russian difficulty to arbitration, writes that he has urged the Prime Minister to adopt the suggestion, "which IS 93 I reasonable, and which, if adopted, I think the whole coun- try would approve."—On Saturday Mr. Bright sent the fol- lowing letter to Mr. Lewis Appleton, of Birmingham, of the International Arbitration and Peace Association :—" Dear sir,—l must ask you to-excuse me from attending your pro- posed meeting. I need not go into the reasons whist) impel I me to this course, but to my mind they seem to be sufficient. I hope your arrangements are such as to secure you a suc- cessful meeting. The Government cannot be damaged by the proposal fer arbitration, and if any opening for reference presents itself I am bound to believe that Mr. Gladstone will not fail to avail himself of it." THE SOLDIERS' AND SAILOR'S' FAMILIES' ASSOCIATION.— This is an association for aiding the wives and families of men of all branches of the land and sea forces of the United Kingdom whilst separated from their husbands and sons by the exigencies of the services. Aid is sought to be rendered—First, by finding suitable employment for those who are ready and willing to help themselves; secondly, by making small temporary grants, where help is actually needed, to all married women, irrespective of their being on the strength of the regiment or not ; thirdly, by aiding aged parents who have been dependent on the help received from their sons when at home. In time of peace the com- mittee hope to be able to help special cases which may, from time to time, be brought to their notice, and which may not come within the qualifications of othe-r charities connectee with the !jolted Services. Subscriptions may be paid to the credit of the fund at Messrs. Coutts and Co.. 99, Strand, London. ACTION BY Mn. W. V. NOBLE HEROISM OF A. SERVANT GIRL AT • FIRE,— THREE LIVES SAVED.—The story of a fire in Uoion-street, Ser- vant in the house, who saved the lives of three of the in- Borough. Loudon, and of the conduct of Alice Ayres, a mates at the sacrifice of her own, will stir all hearts. The fire broke out on Thursday night week, at the house of Mr. li. Chandler, an oil and colour man. Alice Ayres was the first to be awoke by it, and she rushed at Once to the front window and screamed loudly for help. The people in the they stretched out some clothing which would have served street below called to her to jump and save herself, and to break her fall. The flames meanwhile had got hold of the inflammable stock in the shop, and were spread- ing with fearful rapidity. But, amid heat and smoke, and with the prospect before her of death in its most awful shape, Alice Ayres was not to be daunted from her purpose. She first dogged a feather bed to the window and threw it out. It was at once caught up by the people in the street and stretched out below the window. Very soon she appeared at the window again with a little girl in her arms, and with all care threw her down on to the bed. she WAS successful In ibis way in saving three chil- dren from the flames, the first without any hurt from the fall, the second and third with Corns trifling hut, for the great heat and the suff 'citing fumes of the fire were affect- ;pc her, and bad made her hold less firm and her aim less steady. She had now done all that it was possible for her to do, more than she could do with care for her own - safety. The fire had so gained upon her that she must escape at once if she was to escape at all. She sprang accordingly from the window, bu l; in her nervous and exhausted state she missed her mark, jumped short of the bed, and fell heavily on to the pavement. She was picked up and taken to Guy's llospi - tril, where she died on Sunday morning. The proprietor of the shem, his wife and son were burnt to death, and another child was killed by being thrown from the window. The PRIME MINISTER, last night, in an- swer to a question, said there was nothing new to report as to the Afghan frontier dis- pute; but it is ominous that preparations for war are being continued with unwonted vigour. Etores are being sent to Malta and Gibraltar, and other British stations in the Mediterranean, whilst coaling stations in various seas are being fully supplied. There is a rumour current that the AMEER of AFGHANISTAN is indifferent as to the reten- tion of Herat ; but, if this be so, there is irony of fate in his being gazetted last night a Grand Commander of the Star of India. It is persistently reported that the Russians have , advanced beyond Penjdeh ; but such accounts should be received with reserve. There is I no foundation for the rumour of their hav- ing occupied Maruchak—a fact which has caused a feeling to prevail that it may, alter all, be possible to preserve peace. It is asserted with some confidence that the latest proposal of the English Government is to refer the Penjdeh incident to the arbitration of one of the crowned heads of Europe. We trust that this is so ; for if the proposition be rejected by the Russian Government we shall know that they, insist on war; and England will go into the conflict:thrice-armed in having a quarrel that is just.

MR. BIGGAR, M.P., distinguished himself at Warrington on Sunday; he out-Biggared BIGGAR, and that is saying a great deal. His ' attack upon Earl SPENCER was one of so out- rageous a character that we do not hesitate to say there is no country in the world, ex- cept England, that would permit of such I "freedom of speech," and yet the member I for Cavan is amongst those who talk about stifling the voice of the minority. If the LORD•LIRITTENANT thought fit to institute a I criminal prosecution for defamation of char- acter it can hardly be doubted that it would result in Mr. BIGGAR being sent to gaol. But the Imperial authorities have de- termined to let foul tongues wag un- heeded just as local officials disre- gard bad language in the streets, and the result is that Mr BIGGAR is allowed to rage and roam at large. We have reason to believe that many English sympathisers with the cause of Ireland, and not a few Irishmen, were disgusted with the outpour- ing of spleen against the Liberal party to which they were subjected, and went away from the meeting with a feeling bordering on despair. And well they might, if Mr. Btd- GAR were to be accepted as the typical Hiber- nian. But they are not all so immoral, politi- ally, as he makes himself out to be, and we have no fear that they will take his advice and be indifferent as to whether they vote Tory or Liberal at the next election. What a travesty of current events to suggest that there is no difference between one or the other when, within forty-eight hours of the time of his address, English Liberals were speaking and voting in the House of Commons to defeat the insidious attempts of the Tory party to mutilate the Irish Registration Bill as a means of disfranchising a large body of Irish elec- tors! Where is the Church Bill, where is the Land Bill, where is the Franchise Bill that has been given by the Tory party as a boon and a blessing to Ireland ? Instead of con- ferring benefits, the Tories have whipped Irishmen with scorpions, and they will whip them with scorpions again, if they get into power. He must be "blind as never bat was blind" who thinks that the Home Rulers are going to have their own way by coercing the party that happens to he in power after the next election. English statesmen are not to be bought and sold in this easy fashion ; and when politicians like the member for Cavan proclaim that "such a thing as political principle does not exist in England," they say that which sane men reject as untrue; and they need not be sur- prised if the conclusion is come to that those who utter sentiments of this kind are measur- ing a peck out of their own sack. It is ad- visable to look to silver spoons in the presence of an individual who proclaims that he is the only honest man in a nation of rogues. The fact is Mr. BIGGAR has over- shot his mark in coming to Warrington, and , the result cannot but be to set Irishmen thinking of the gulf, especially on Irish questions, which separates the average Liberal from the average Tory. Irritated at times they may be that the remedy for wrongs is so slow-footed, but they are not wholly ungrate- ful for what the Liberal party has done for them nor are they so destitute of principle as to accept the bad advice which is given them by Mr. BIGGAR.

SUDDEN DEATH IN I TRAlN.—Testerchy afternoon Mrs. Agnes Ferguson, aged 80 years, a widow, who had resided at 36, Carlton-road, Birkenhead, died under the following painful circumstances. It appears that she had been stay- ing about two months on a visit to her sister at Whalley Range, Manchester, and in her company was returning to Birkenhead. At the Central Station, Manchester, at 2-30 p.m. she complained of feeling ill, and was assisted to the train by a porter. When the train started is move she said -"What if I should die! I feel so ill," and immediately fell backwards into her sister's arms. She kept in that poeition without moving until the arrival of the train at Warrington 'Central Station at 2-50 p.m., when a Manchester medical Igentleman, who was travelling in another Portion of the 'same train, was requested to see her, and he at once pro- nounced that the poor lady was dead. He add,(l that pro- bably heart disease was the cause of death. Deceased had been troubled with palpitation of the heart, but had not been medically attended for it. The body was at once removed to the Ram's Head Hotel, near by, to await an inquest, and the police were communicated with. DESPERATE LEAP FROM A TukiN.—The particulars of a desperate leap from a train were revealed at Warrington Borough Court, yesterday awning, when a young man named Richard Bower, of Widnse, was charged before Mr. ' John White and Mr. Z. Armitage with leaving a train' whilst in motion, on the 20;ti ult.—Detective Inspecter Simpson said that on the date name,l the defendant was a passenger on the Cheshire Lines Railway, and had come fecam Sheffield on a journey to Widnes. He was acceru- panied,hy his mother. and the two changed trains at War- rington, where they waited for the 9 8 p.m. train to Widnes. They had several articles of luggage with them, including a small black bag, and when tleey entered the train they left the luggage behind them. He believed it was true that the black bag contained over £lOO. When the train had gone a considerable distance the defendant missed the bag. He then at oncs opened the doer and jumped out of the train, between the carriage and the wall. It was a great , mercy that he was not killed, and the cerripeny felt bound to take proceedings.—A railway official spoke to seeing de- fendant afterwards. He was injured about the knee, scar- red on the head, and the clothes were Cu'. Defendant said I that it was &question of money or tire. The property was afterwards found all right.— Mr. Knowles, Widnes, who appeared for the defendant, said that his client had been in business some time time at Sheffield. and the money in the bag was the Soint savings of himself and his mother. If they Bad lost it they would have been reduced to poverty. He submitted that anyone under the circumstances would have become desperate and leaped from the train. The railway . authorities were right in prosecuting in these cases, but he thought that the circumstances connected with the present one were such as to justify the magistrates in dismissing the case on plyment of costs—The Bench took that view, and Mr. Simpson remarking that he did not wish to press the case, the defendant was only ordered to pay 12e, the costs.

LOCAL CASEI AT THE TIVERATIL ASSIZES —On Wednes- day Lawrence Cools, aged 25, labourer, for having at Eccles- ton, on the 27th February' committed a burglary at the dwelling-house of William Hooper, and Stolen therefrom a clock and other articles, was sentenoed to six month's im- prisonment with hard labour.--Patrick M•Cabe, 18, a la- bourer, was indicted for having at Widnes, on the 15th March last-, feloniously assaulted and robbed Michael Mar! phy.—A defence of mistaken identity was raised by Mr. Segar, and the jury acquitted the prisoner.--Rainford Coal Company a Stewart and Beswiek..—This was an action in the Nisi Prius Gnarl, on Wednesday, before Mr. Justice Wills and a common jury, to recover the suns of LGO for goods sold and delivered.—Mr. Picaford was counsel for the plaintiffs, and the defendants, who are coal meschan's, carrying on business at Sandhills, Liverpool, were repre- sented by Mr. Collins, QC , with whom woe Mr. Walton. The plaintiffs had supplied the defendants with coal from their collieries, situate near St. Helens, for the greater part of last yen., and the sum claimed repre- sented the amount of the account rendered for the month of December last, the payment of which was due on the 21st January. The defendants' case was that the c)al supplied by the plaintiffs, which is known as the Rainford 4ft. and sft , was of such inferior quality that they had sustained serious loss by the falling off of custom, and they put in a counter claim for damages for loss of trade. For the plain- tiffs, however, it was c 'Wended that the coal sold was of the quality demanded, and that if it were of an unsatisfac- tory kind, the defendants were under no obligation to con- tinue to trade with the plaintiffs. A number of witnesses were called on both sides to give evidencs as to the quality of the coal bought from the defendants. An export, named Efird, called on behalf of the defendants to testify to the in- ferior quality of samples of the coal supplied to them by the plaintiffs, said in cross-examination that there was not a better coal in Lancashire than the Rainford 4-foot, either for domestic purposes or coke making ; but the Rainford 5-foot was a bad coal. The jury found for the plaintiffs for die amount claimed.

ACTION FOR DAM WES AGAINST TILE BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION CORPANY —At the Chester County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Horatio Uoyd, Ann Longhand, guardian and next friend of Michael Doran, an infant seven years of age, residing in Mersey-street. Run- corn, sought to recover damages of £lOO from the Bridge- water Navigation Company, for injuries alleged to have been sustained by the infant Doran through the negligence of the defendants' servants. Mr. Lloyd, in opening his statement, explained that the defendants had a yard in Mersey-street which had a sliding gate, fitted with a beam , along the top, the end of which' entered a slot in the wall when the gate was closed, and thus secured it. On the 13th December, the infant plaintiff was playing with other chil- dren on the pavement near the gate. One of the company's servants was wheeling a barrow-load of timber through the gateway, when the wheelbarrow, or part of the wood on it, caught the gate, which fell on the top of the child, inflicting very serious injury to it. One of its legs was broken, and it had received severe injuries to the head, necessitating lie being under medical attendance for el_rlot weeks. It was obviously the duty of the defendants to see that the gate was kept in each proper repair that it would not be danger- ous for ordinary passersby'. Evidence having been given, the jary gave a verdict for the plaintiff, awarding damages of £7o.—Mr. Fletcher made an application for execution to _ _ _
• be stayed on the ground of excessive datnagee.—The Judge granted the application.

—,- I THEFT OF COAL AT WIDNES —At Widnes Petty Sea. clone, on Wednesday, Mary Riley, a young woman was charged with stealing 6Slbs. of coal, worth sd, the property of the Appleton Q tarry Company. About 10 o'clock on Saturday night, P.C. Almond was on duty in Deacea-road, and saw a person near the coal heap in the quarry. He found the prisoner there with a bucket full of coal. She said she was only getting a little coal to light the fire.—The prisoner was sentenced to a month's imprisonment. div.p: RUNCORN FOOTBALL CLUB.

The annual meeting of thin club was held in the large room at Wilson's Hotel, on Monday evening. 'There was a large attendance of tnembers. Mr. W. Brookes was voted to the chair. Mr. J. E. Langshaw presented the annual report The club, he stid, had on the whole boos very successful, both in rezard to the matches played and its financial con- dition during the past season. He remarked with gratifica- tion upon the fact that in both teams the players had turned up with great regularity. The first team bad played 28 matches, won 17, drawn five, and lost air. They bad scored 14 goals, 33 tries, and 53 minor points, agtinat their opponents 4 goals, 17 tries, and 64 minor points. The mat- ches lost were with Aspell, Mossley, Sale, St. Clements, Warrington, and Tottingtoo. The players who obtained tries were H. Hughes 11, G. Andrews 8, T. Johnsm 4, 11. Speakman 3, G. Wainwright 2, R. Roberts 2. and W. Paged. Dean, W. Wright, W. 11. Broady, H. Wright, J. Hofflancl, J. Clarke, J. Galley, J. Barnes, T. Woods, and J. Lewis kicked one each. Of the 41 tries obtained only 8 were converted into goals. 11. Speakman kicked five goals from tbe &id of play—(loud applause)—and T. Woods one. The second team had played 24 matches, of which 15 were won, and 9 drawn. They were not defeated on any occasion. (Appliule ) They had scored 2.3 goals, 33 tries, and 96 minor point., against their opponents 2 goals, 7 , tries, and 19 minor points. The tries were obtained be 1 J. B. Clarke 9, E. Lunt 8, G Whitby 7, J. Janion 5, G. Wainwright 4, E. Andrews 4, T. Abrams 4, W. Antrobus 3, W. Riley, E. Orme, H. Andrews 2 Isiah ; and J. Gittens, J. Stubbs, J. Galley, T. Woods, R. 11,berts, 11. Ltncaster, and ,1 T. Cox. W. A. Riley dropped one goal from the field. Of the 57 tries obtained 21 were converted into goals. Mr. IC , Johnson presented the treasurer's report. It appeared the club started the season with a balance in hand of £2O 93 101 The honorary subscriptions amounted to £7 15s 6d; mem- bers' subscaiptims £23 Ils 63, gate money £2ll 63 43— (loud applause)—other items bringing the income to £264 Os 21. (Applause.) The expenditure amounted to £l9O , Os 51, including £O4 7s for players' expenses, £l6 14s 411 for refreshmen's. £8 17 101 for stamps, telegrams, and src- retary'a salary .£l6 14s 41, £6 19s 81 for new tent, £7 Os Si for advertising, £27 7584 for field expenses (including rent), £l6 13s 61 for stationery and printing, £3 Ns 6d for doc- tor's expenses for maimed members, £l3 4s 31 for gate keepers. div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER..
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER..

LONDON, TarnsDAY. To position of affairs in relation to Russia has within the week distinctly deepened in gravity. As lug as there was any room to believe Russia did not desire war there was hope for peace. The VLIV3 of our own Government are clearly formed, and have not differed from the first. Mr. Gladstone, as is acknowledged all over Europe, in the glow- ing encomiums of his speech on MondaY night, not only does not desire war, but within due limits aff cting the honour of England laboura.for peace. It only required that the Russians should be animated by the same spirit to insure a peaceful solution f the question. But it is now clear beyond controvery that Russia has made up her mind for war. It is with the unfortunate Czar as it wes with Napoleon the Third in 1870. The Czar ia fighting not for India. but for his own throne. Russia is in the cor dition of a desperate and despairing man to whom no change can bring added misery. Almost a bankrupt, always standing on the brink of revolution, Russia staggers along Things cannot be worse than they are, and son-allow or other a war may make them better. At any rate, whilst the country is engaged in a great struggle the Nihilists must needs keep quiet. Thus the Czar and his Government reason, and thus two great countries are, not drifting, but steaming into war.

Under these solemn circumstances, on the eve of what may prove the most momentous war the world hasalseen, it is a supreme satisfaction to Englishmen to be able, as Mr. Gladstone put it in his speech of Monday night, to " chal- ledge the verdict of civilieed mankind whether we have not done all that men could do by every just and honourable effort to prevent the plunging of two countries, with all the millions that own their sway into bloodshed and strife." England owes an immense debt to Mr. Gladstone, but not the least imposiug item in it is tha position from which this country will advance to war if war it must be. For the last three days the continental papers commenting on the speech of Monday have been full'of expressions of unqualified ad- miration and respect for the attitude assumed by England in comparison with that displayed by Russia. The magni- tioent outburst of elrquence of Monday night did more than conquer the House of Commons though that is a ra7e achievement. I overca ne the prejudices of Europe and placed England in a povition prouder to hold than if her arms had won a great victory.

- - I have been much struck in reading the comments in foreign papers to note the universality and persistence of the references to Mr. Gladstone's age. Several speak of him as the "aged statesman," and make references to " this crowning achievement of his closing years." It is a signi- ficant fact that we who lice in his presence, see and hear him every day, never think of him as an old elan. Itewas remarkable on Monday nieht how, as the speech went for- ward, he seeintel to renew his life like the eagle. He had sat for two hours battled and annoyed by the preliminary skirmishing which the groat Conservative party maintained under the leadership of Mr. Arthur O'Connor. He was suf- fering from a severe cold, and, worse than all, he had to explain away the Soudan campaign and announce its proximate close. This was a combination of circumstances hard to struggle against, more especially when there was added to it the constant interruptions of Mr. Ashmead Bartlett and Lord Randolph Churchill, which dispropor- tionately irritate the Premier. But when be reached the , portion of his speech devoted to Russia be rose to the sub- limest heights of oratory. In the fervour of the moment he had ecreq aered even his physical weakness. 'lh3 hoarse- ness. instead of following its natural course of increasing. had miraculously disappeared, and his voice rang out full and clear al be described how England, earnest in the cause of peace, was yet resolute and ready if need be for war. There is no ptrallel in Parliamentary history for what followed on the conclusion of this address. Commenced before a hostile audience, whose anger was increased by his seething criticism on the policy of 187 S, he worked it up to a pitch of patriotic enthusiasm, in the heat of which pitiful party tactics were burned up like chaff in a furnace. For a moment—
None were for a party, but all were for the State, and amid prolonged cheering, in which Conservatives joined with Liberals, the vote was carried by acclama- tion.

With respect to the curious incident in the House of Commons on Friday night when Mr. Gladstone read half a telegram from Sir Evelyn Baring ender the impression that it was a complete message, many stories are recalled of similar misapprehensions arising from misconstrued tele- grams. One of the funniest I hear from an attachi of the Italian Embassy here. It seems that Lord Palmerston was always spokes of in Ittlian Ministerial cirelts by the dim- inutive ‘• Palmer." It was the habit of Count C4VOILIr to spend a good deal of his leisure time in the telegraph office at Turin. Ile was thus engaged on the 14. h of June, Issflo when he stumbled upon a telegram in th 3 following words : " Palmer hung this morning. lyeclared he went to the sclffold a murdered man." The shock to Count Cavour was momentarily severe, but ha was presently rea3sured by having it explained to him that the paragraph did not refer to the great English statesman, but to the Hugely mur- derer.

For London Society the House of Commons rules the pronunciation of debateable words in respect of foreign names and places which, In these troublesome times, ate always cropping up. There is one word upon the pronuncia- tion of which an important divisicn of opinion exists. This is the wo-d "gerrymander." Mr. Gladstone and all English members pronounce the word as if spelt with a j. Mr. Parnell, to the amusement and astonishment of the !dense, always pronounces the word with the g hard. In this case Mr. Parnell is undoubtedly right. The word is of very re- cent origin and can be infallibly traced. , In the early days of the American Benublic there was an official named E/d- -ridge Gerry, who was entrusted with the official marking of boundaries in the State of Massachusets. He was accused of manipulating the boundazies for political purposes. hence the word gerrymander. Gerry, by the way, lived for some time at Elmwood, Boston, now the home of Mr. Russell Lowell, from whom, I may add, I hare this authoritative settlement of a question that even amid the clash of arms much disturbs the House of Commons.

This is the great picture week, all the galleries being now open, though the public must wait till Monday for their glimpse at the Academy. Having seen both the Academy and the Grosvenor, I find the latter the more in- teresting. 'there are, perhaps, half a dozen pictures at Burlington House worthy of the Academy's fame. But there is what Mr. Bright might call an appalling residuum. The larger gallery at the Grosvenor is full of contrasts and oppositions—perhaps none more striking than between the, two pictures to which ire assigned the places of honour, Mr. Watts has a very beautiful allegory of love and life. One knows his figures—the sylph-like young girl and the cupid scarcely boyish—the delicate colour, and the wide- ness of the remove from any common-place truth.

Alma Tadema is in force and variety. There is an ex- tremely disagreeable picture of a doctor feeling a patient's pulse, and certainly if the doctor seems unsympathetic to the patient, the artist has been most unsympathetic to the doctor, who looks common-place and vulgar and uniotetes- ting. On the other hand there are some lovely little bits of old classic life where, in treating marble glistening in sunshine, and the blue of southern seas and skies, this arti.et shews that with many followers he is still without a rival. A painter scarcely likes to be called the follower even of such a master as Tadessa. Mr. E. M. Hale has taken the kind of subject Tadema would delight in, and has made it intel- ligible and artistically agreeable. "In the days of Phidias " It was as the model stood in her pretty fresh costume, and it was as the sculptor worked, his nether le Its even less em- berraseed than a IlighlandeCe. Frank Hall has one very fins portrait of the late Lord Overstone. As which has told, and diseases as well as ate, on the frame has yet left the lice keen and c_haracteristic, and the eyes bright with iatelligencs. Frank- 101 l is pre-eminently the painter for faces which have strength rather than loveliness, and Watts for beauty where force would be a blemish. Carlyle called the portrait Watts took of Lim a flayed horse," but nothing can be lovelier than the girlish face and graceful figure of Miss Rachel Gurney (No. 82) This room is not very strong in landscapes. Mark Fisher is scarcely represented. Thomas Farrer has but a small

moonlight subject, very sweet in effect, but its strength is in subject and portrait. Richard Doyle has been se long the presiding genius of 'bat little tank of a room devoted to water colours, that the apartment seems dull without him. But there is good work upon its walls. It is impossible to enter the rem without being artested at the door by Mr. J. M. Donna's" Coning home of the goats." In the ren- dering of Swiss mountain scenery this painter has scarcely a rival In this country. His work is always thought out and true to nature, and he keeps modestly within the re_ sources of his palette. Thus his Alpine pictures always have the charm and never the vulgarity which often spoils Elijah Walton's work. Tristram Ellis has this year brought wita him a good harvest from his wanderings in Portugal. These handsome girls in the market boats, f ull of die, and Youth, and vigour, ano as great a pleasare to look at as if we saw them un ter those hot suns, bending to the oar or bursting into merry laughter with their gossips in the boat. To much of the sickly sentimentality, Which goes by the name of art, this laborious painter's work is an aiwirable tonic.

div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SITURDA.Y—Baore Alderman Burgess. A DESEETEEL—WiIIiam Ellison was charged with being a • deserter tam a regiment of foot stationed at Salford. He pleaded guilty and was committed to Walton Gaol to await an escort. ALLEGED THEET.—A lad. named Thomas Troy was charged with having stolen a pigeon on Friday morning the property of Edwin Jones, 19, Erwood-street. He was re- manded till Monday. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison), Mr. Greening, and Mr. John Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS.—The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness :—Robert Once, Arplev-road, on Satur- day evening, fined 55, including costs; Mary Ellen Wilkin- son, in Bridge-street, on Saturday, fined 10e and costs ; Martin Duffy, in D,dman'e-laue, on Sunday morning, dis- charged on promising to leave the town; Thomas Maanion, in Horsemerket-street, fined 53 and costs; Robert Dakin, 68th appearance, at Market Gate, on the 18th ult, fined 5s and costs; Michael Quinn, in Horsemarket-street, on the 18th ult, fined 103 and cools; Joseph Patchett, in Sankey- street, on the. 20th ult, fined 54 and costs; M.chael Connor and Bridget Higgins, in Bridge-street, on the 20th ult, dis missed with a caution ; Ellen Roberts, in Winwick-road, on the 20th tilt, fined 5s and costs.--Edward Crosby, for being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street, and as- saulting Mteearet Fleming, a woman well known to the Court, was sent to prison for a month, and a like penalty was imposed upon Bridget Lally, an unfortunate, for inde- cent behaviour in Cockbedgeelane.—John Finegan was fined 103 and costs for assaulting Martin Burns in 1884.-- James Bowcock, for using abusive and obscene language in the Market Hell, on the 15._1a ult, was fined 103 and costs. --For crying fish for site, in the market, contrary to the bve-laws, James Bibby was fined 53 and costs.--James Harris, for being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and cart in Sankey-street, on the 20th ult, was fined 5s and coste.-- Samuel Heath was fined 103 and costs, or fourteen days in prison, for keeping lodgers without having his house regis- tered. THEFT or A PlGEON.—Thomas Trey, a boy, was charged, with stealing a pigeon, value is, from a cote belonging to Edward Jones, 19. Erwood-street, on or about the 24th ult. —He pleaded guilty, and was sentenced to seven days' im- prisonment. ALLOWING A NUISANCE.—Arthur Theodore Moult was summoned by Inspector Norman in respect to nuisances, arising from defective draihage, on property belonging to him in Brideewater-street.—fle was ordered to abate the nuisance within seven days, or be liable to a penalty of £1 a day afterwards. Scaoot ATTENDANCE CAsits.—Mr. George Riley obtained convictions in the following cases :—William Nunnerley, engine driver, taill-street ; James Lee, labourer, Heath- side; Mary Bennett (vela) had not paid school fees for three months, and who behaved in a very boisterous manner in court) ; John Howard, Hall-street; and Robert Kelly, Sharp-street. TUESDAY—Before Mr. C. Broadbent. DRUNKENNESS.—A woman named Annie McCarthy was fined 5s and costs for being drunk the previous evening. WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Pickmere and Mr. John Fairclough. MISCELLANEOUS.—Lucy Lynch, last from Runcorn, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street the previous morning. She was cautioned and dismissed. —James Hill, last from Dublin, was committed to Walton gaol to await escort, he having admitted being a deserter from Her Maj sty's 2nd Battalion Liverpool Regiment, stationed at the Curragh, on the 23rd inst.--Thomas Handley, a reserve man, was charged with being drunk in Buttermarket-street on the previous evening.—Eie was dis- missed with a reprimand.—Lawrence Duane, 2, Heath- lane, Golborne-street, was fined 5s for cruelly striking a donkey about forty times, with a stick, on the 11th inst. THURSDAY.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster, • and Mr. John Platt. DRUNKENNESS —John Hodgscn was fined 5s and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Winwick-street on the pre- vious evening.—James Anderson, a reserve man, was -charged with a similar offence, and wan let off on payment o is, the lock-up fee.—Michael Connor was eent to prison for a month for being drunk and disorderly in Cockbedge- lane on the previous evening. —Thomas Sweeney, a reserve man, was charged with riding from Manchester to War- rington, on the Cheshire Lines Railway, without a ticket ; he was also charged with being drank on the premises of the Committee. On the arrival of the 11 o'clock evening train from Manchester prisoner could not produce his ticket and was 80 drunk that he had to be lifted out of the car- riage. Subsequently a ticket was found on the floor of the carriage, and in COllB,quence Detective-Superintendent Simpson withdrew the firat charge. At the suggestion of the Bench the second ene also was withdrawn, and prisoner was let off with a caution. FRIDAY —Before Mr. John White and Mr. Z. Armitage. MISCELLANEOUS —Simeon Urmston was fined 2e 61 and -coats for stone-throwing in Lythgoe's-lane, on the 28th ult., and John Kelley, John Bibby, and Richard Coffee, for com- mitting a similar offence in Winwick-street, on the 28th nit., were ordered to pay 23 6.1 each, or receive six strokes each with the birch rod.—John Hargretves was charged with assaulting his wife. Louisa, on the 26th April, and was ordered to find a surety for his good behaviour for six months.—Emma Stretford was summoned by Michael Rogers, who claimed from her as his apprentice the sum of 13s, in consequence of her neglect of work. The Bench ordered defendant to pay 103, including the costs, at the rate of 6,1 per week.—Jac)le Humphries was charged with assaulting his wife Elizabeth, and was ordered to be bound over in £lO, and find a Flinty in a like amount, to be of good behaviour for six months. MASTER AND Wouxateee—Joseph Simcock was sum- mo led by John Dixon, inspector of the Cheshire Lines Tele- graphic Department, for assaulting hien on the 28th nit.— Dixon said the defendant was working under him as a joiner, and on the day in question refused to do some wcrk when ordered. Dixon then told kim he would have to leave, and, words having passed between them, Simcock struck him and knocked him down. Dixon admitted mak- ing an cffensive remark to defendant, and Mr. Davies, who appeared for the defendant, said that the provocation received was sufficient to cause the defendant, who WAS a quick tempered man, to lose control of his temper.—He was ordered to find a surety of £lO, and be bound over, hireeelf in £5, to keep the peace for six months.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. MONDAY.—Befare M r. F. H. Gossage. DiatrenoNsrass.—For this offence the following persons -were fined :—Mary Riley, Mary Daley, Martin Cavannagrb, John McShane, Patrick Regan, William Smith, Patrick Feeney, Ann Holland, John Myber, John Mannion, and Michael Morley. WAERIORS.—SamueI Smith and Edward Tracey, for ghting in Widnes-road on Satarday night, were bound over to keep the peace for two months.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. i. Brock. DRUNEENNESS.—The following persons were fined for this offence :—John Lotthouse, John Bentley, Margaret Lucy Jones, Martin Grady, and Thomas Hunt. BREACHES OF THE PEACF, —Agnes Newton and Elizabeth Mason were charged with committing a breach of the peace in Beamont-street, on the 17th ult. P.C. Cummins heard the disturbance half a mile away. They were bound over to be of good behaviour for two months.—Bridget Cooney, a married woman, was dea,t with in a similar manner for Creating a disturbance in Sutton's-lane, on the 19th ult.— Mary Platt pleaded guilty to committing a breach of the Peace in New-street, on the 23rd ult , and sue was bound over for two months. PITCH AND Toss.—James Cowley and Lawrence Gasheen, youths, were charged with playing pilch and toss in Sut- ton's-lane, on the 19th ult. P.C. Savory proved the case. Gasheen was fined Is and costs, 7s 61, and Cowley, who aid ant appear, wan fined 2s 6I and costs. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—James Johnson, of Appleton Vil- lage, was fined Is and costs, 4s, for allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire.

div.p: RITNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. Mom) Ay.—Before Mr. W. Bankes and Mr. James Reynolds. .

PROFANE LANGUAGE —John Bcameo, a boatman, Was charged with having, on the 22nd April, used obsceno and profane langnage in Coopepstreet.—On the evidence of P.C. Eason, the defendant, who made his eleventh appear- ance, was fined 103 and costs, 93 6 I. BREA -CH OF THE CANAL BOATS BlLL,—Ftichard Fox, canal carrier, Whai" Bridge, was summoned by the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority for allowing a boat to be used on the Bridgewater Canal Which was not " marked, lettered, or numbered," according to the provisions of the Canal Boats Act. —lnspector Farrington prove' the case, and the defen- dant was fined 5s and Costs, 13s. Ocycazas.-7-John Lang, an old man, was charged with begging in High:street, on the previous night. The prisoner, who 123'1 acted in a violent manner to those persons who
had refused him alms, w,.s committed to gaol for a month. —John Tabener, a rough-looking young fellow, was sen- tenced to 14 days' hard labour for sleeping in Mr. S. Crosby's stable on Sunday night.

DARESBURY PETTY SES'IONS. TIIESDAY.—Before Mews. E. Greenell, W. Long, James Marson, and W. C. Jones. DRONEENNESS.—John Moore was fined 53 and costs for having been drunk and disnrderly at Appleton, on the 19th April ; John Rutter was fined 5s and costs for a similar offence at Appleton, on the 19,h April; Thomas Robinson. for a like-offence at Walton Superior. on the 11th April, was fined 5s and costs. ILLEGAL REMOVAL OF SWINE.—WiIIiaM Williams, a pig I dealer, belonging to Chester, was charged with having caused ten pigs to be removed from Warrington Pig Market through an infected circle at Appleton, without a licence, on the 25th March. Mr. Wellhead, of Warrington, defended, and contended that sufficient notice of the order declaring the infected circle had not been given.—The Bench, how- ever, considered that the defendant, being a pig dealer, was much tceblarne in not acquainting himself with the orders issued. He would be fined 20s and costs, but if the offences were repeated he would be fined heavily. STRAYING CarrLE.—Joseph Hyam was fined 2s and costs for having allowed a pony to stray on the highway at Appleton on the 19th April ; and Ann Bate was ordered to pay 49 61 costs for having allowed a cow and heifer to stray on the highway at Appleton on the aims day. SAVAGE DOGS.—Joseph Smith was charged with not I keeping two dogs under proper control on the 6th April.— P.O 186 said that on the night of the Bth April he was passing defendant's house, when a black retriever dog run at him, bit him, and tore his coat.—J. Bushel, G. Whittier, Fanny Bennett, and Thomas Bushell each spoke to having been attacked by the dog referred to by the constable and another dog belonging to defendant —As the attacks by the latter had, however, not occurred recently, the defendant was only ordered to keep the retriever dog under proper control, and to pay costs. A SANITARY OFFENCE.—Ezra Gandy was summoned for having permitted a new house at Seven Oaks to be occupied without having provided a sufficient supply of wholesome water.—He was fined Is and cos. ALLEGED THEFT OF A DuCg.—Peter Chadwlck, of Ncrth- wich, was charged with having stolen two ducks, the pro- perty of Jacob Milling•on, on the 30th March ; and there was also a charge against him of baying purchased one duck, knowing it to have been stolen. It appeared that two ducks had been stolen from complainant's premises, and one of them was afterwards found in the prisoner's posses- sion. The latter stated that he had bought the dock from a tramp whose name he did not know, and had given him Is 61 for it. This statement was corroborated by a female witness.—The Bench, after warning the prisoner not to buy ducks from tramps again, and stating tliat it was a very sus- picious case, dismissed the charges.

div.head: ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.
div.p: THE ROYAL VISIT TO IRELAND.

- - - • It was raining hard at eleven o'clock on Friday morning when the Prince and Princess of Wales quitted the Royal yacht Osborne, in Carrickfergus Roads, and steamed to Belfast in the steamer Manx Qeeen and there was every indication of a very wet day. This;however, did not deter a great crowd assembling in the vicinity of Donegal Quay, where the first ceremonial of the day took place. '1 be Manx Queen steamed up alongside the quay shortly after twelve o'clock, where a body of the Harbour Commissioners was assembled, and they presented an address congratulating the Prince on hisevisit to the prosperous and thriving capital of Ulster, accompanied by the Princess. His Royal High- ness took his stand on a raised platform in the shed on the quay, the crowds in the streets near by and the company surrounding the platform cheering meanwhile, and suitably replied. The Prince afterwards declared the quay open, and visited several of the principal manufactories in the town. On arriving at Derry on Saturday, the Prince and Princess of Wales met with an enthusiastic demonstration. The approaches to the station were filled with the towns- people, while the Mayor and the Corporatien, the repre- sentatives of the Apprentice Boys, and the public bodies formed a procession, the Prince and Princess and Prince Albert Victor following, escorted by a troop of the Royal Deagoons and a company of the Somerset regiment. The streets through which the procession passed were crowded with a cheering multitude. At the Court House a dozen addresses were presented to the Prince, and in reply his Royal Highness said he hoped that at no distant date the Princess of Wales and himself might be able to again visit Ireland. The Royal party afterwards drove round the walls of the city, and lunched at the Bishop's palace before proceeding on their way to Baronscourt. Addresses were presented from the Port and Harbour Commissioners and other local bodies, and great crowds surrounded the station displaying flags and b inners, and accompanied by bands from various Orange and Conservative lodges.—The visit was brought to a close on Monday morning, when their Royal Highnesses quitted Baronsc,urt, where they had been staying as guests of the Hake and Duchess of Abercorn since Saturday, accompanied on their departure by the warmest demonstrations of devotion and loyalty by the tenantry and inhabitants of Newtownstewart The Princess wore the same dress of dark green Irish poplin which she wore when she landed at Kingstown, and appeared to be greatly refreshed by the two days' Lest she ha-1 enjoyed at Baronscourt. One of the last and most characteristic acts of the Princess during her stay was to visit the bed. se of a dying child the daughter of Mr Murphy, a churchwarden of Baronscourt Chapel—and her Royal Highness sat for some time with the little creatnre before it breathed its last. Thoueands of people assembled at Omagh and dungannon to show their loyalty and pvsent addresses of welcome to the Prince. While the train stool at Omegh, however, re small bend of about 100 peasants, bearing flege and pieces of black calico on sticks, made their appearance about a quarter of a mile off. A body of the loyalists set off to meet them, and on the approach of the latter they ig- nominiously threw down some of their flags and ran away across the fields, with the loyelists after theta, and they were effectually dispersed. At Cookstosvx the Royal patty left the train and walked round the station, wh'cis was crowded, and surrounded by an enthusiastic mob, which gave the Prince an exceptionally warm reception. The de- parture was made at a quarter-past one, and the train passed along the banks of Loci; Neagh, on the way Is Carrickfer- gus. A few strips of black bunting were displayed from a field near Castleclawson, tozether with a couple c.f poles crossed to represent a gibbet. Thousands assembled at the

WARRINGTON FIRST ELEVEN V. NEXT SIXTEEN AND DENTON.—Tbe opening match of the Warrington Club was played on Saturday between two teams selected as above. A heavy storm of rain in the morning and several showers during the progress of the game contributed to make the ground very soft. Notwithstanding the soft wicket the ground played truly, and a good game resulted in a win for the eleven with twenty runs and four wickets to spare. The sixteen won the toss, and commenced batting at 245 pm. Denton and Knowles faced the bowling of the brothers Lawton. A maiden over from C. G. Lawton was bowled against Denton, and J. C. took the ball. His first delivery was returned by Knowles, and that player I gave way to Smith, who was sent back with the next ball. In striking to leg he over-reached the ball and put it in the slips. Unswortb, the next corner, was almost run out by a smart return from cover point, and two balls later Denton had a similar narrow escape from the same position. Care- ful play by Denton added two to the score. In attempting to run for an off drive, Denton was forestalled by the senart fielding from Clark, and was run out. The game looked black for the sixteen, the register showing 3,3, 2. Wignall, however, enlivened the game, and, by dashing play, put on twelve. With the exception of Voisey, Taylor, and Pod- more, only moderate play was displayed by the remainder, and the innings closed for 57. The bowling of Messrs. Lawton and the wicket•keeping of Armstrong were the chief features of the innings, and they deserved the plau- dits of the spectators. After the usual interval, Fairclough and Wallington began the battle for the eleven, Smith and Denton bowling. Fairclough got two long hits to leg, but with the score at 14 he was run out. England joined Wallington, and steady play by both ensued. Smith obtained both wickets, and C. G. Lawton and 'Clarks were partners. Clark cut Denton to the boundary for three fours in the next few overs, and was then caught at wicket. Armstrong followed, and good cricket was shown. Lawton was caught from a long htt to leg by Podmore running hard with one hand low down. This bit of fielding was the finest of the day, and Podmore re- ceived a hearty round of applause. When stumps were drawn at half-past six J. C. Lawton and Hind appeared well se. Owing to the soft ground and the large number of fielders, run-getting was a slow and difficult process of the eleven.

Forty cases had been re- ceivel during the past seven days at the Mensal! Hospital, and there were now under treatment 119 ca9es. LOCAL SELF•CrOTERNMRNT.—Sir Charles Dilke presided on Wednesday evening at the annual meeting of the Mid- dlesex Liberal Association, at the City Liberal Club, and delivered a brief, address. He slid Liberals were never more united with reference to all those questions of home policy which lay in the near future, although of course they could not exclude speculative opinion as to what might be beyond. The right hon. baronet added that he attached great importance to local self-government in its wideSt SeNe as the key to many of the questions with which Parliament would shortly have to deal. Regarding the more urgent questions of, foreign policy, he believed both Liberals and Conservatives were agreed, as exempli- fied in the House of Commons in a remarkable manner after Mr. Gladetolm's speech on the vote of credit. THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL
MONDAY.

The cross-examination of Mr. Collier, assistant manager of the Bridgewater Canal, by Mr. Pember, Q.C., was con- tinued. Witness said he estimated that 900,000 tone barge traffic and 500,000 foreign and coastwise would have to cross the ship canal annually to get to the Bridgewater. About 75 barges and 9 small ships a day used the Bridge. water Canal. He was aware that when the ship canal was made the Bridgewater barges would he able to enter it at any state of the tide, whilst at present they could not get out with under six feet of water. It was the down traffic particularly which would be delayed, and the free user of the ship canal, under such circumstances, would not abso- lutely remove the difficulty. The canal was larger, and the traffic could not be worked at the same speed as it could upon the tideway of the estuary ; and the result of that would be that it would arrive at Liverpool too late to be docked in the same tide. At present they got all their traffic down on the same tide. The capabilities of the Bridgewater Canal were not yet reached, but they preferred to improve the Mersey and Irwell Navigation, which they intended to do. They proposed to deepen this naviption, shorten it, and reduce the number of locks, which would have the effect of shortening the journey between Liverpool and Man- chester. The company bad autherised the directors to carry out the works he had referred to. This authority was given in January or February last, and since that time contracts had been let involving works to the amount ef £25,000, the contracts at present in hand being for about £5,000 Mr. John Meadowcrof', agent for the Bridgewater Canal Company at Runcorn Docks, said the canal, if made, would have a very serious effect on their business. The Bridge- water Company worked a fixed traffic, everything being arranged by time. It was well known when the last train of barges would leave, and they took their departure from Manchester punctually. He bad known cases when a barge had lost a tide he had put the goods on the raile so that there should be no loss of time in the delivery of them, and this was necessary to carry on the competition and meet the wishes of the traders. If the canal were made, he be- lieved this speedy traffic would be absolutely destroyed. The Bridgewater Company carried on operations all night, so far as the barge traffic was concerned, but the ships pre- ferred to do their work in daylight. He attached just as much importance to the inward traffic as to the outward, particularly to that which went beyond Manchester, namely, to Rochdale, Todmorden, and other places in that direction.—Mr. Garnett, piermaster at Runcorn, gave similar evidence.—Mr. Wiswall, CE., said he was engineer to the Bridgewater Canal Company. He considered the proposed embankment with the single entry into the estuary ' at Runcorn would have a very damaging effect on the work- ing of the existing navigationa—Sir F. Bramwell was re- called upon this part of the case, and approved of the scheme for improving the navigation, which, he said, would put an end to the floods along the line of the Mersey. and Irwell, and would form a good and efficient waterway for the traffic. The increased current and other surroundings would keep the river open with less dredging than was now required, and be thought the estimate of MOO.OOO sufficient for the proposed works. '

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

Mr. Bartholomew, general manager of the Aire and Cal- der Navigation, was the first witnems examined on Tuesday, and his evidence Was to the effect that the improvements proposed to be carried out in the Mersey and Irwell would meet all the requirements of the trade by water between Manchester and Liverpool, and that the larger scheme of the ship canal was not needed.—Mr. Saunders then ad- dressed the Committee on behalf of the Bridgewater Navi- gation Company, and objected to the company being corn- pelted to sell their undertaking to the promoters, as it had not been proved that they bad failed to carry out their obliga- tions to the public.—Mr. Littler, Q.C., for the Runcorn Commissioners, urged that the traders should have a free use of the canal if it should be made.—Mr. Robert Shaw, the chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, , examined by Mr.MeyseyThompsen,produced the resolution Passed by the merchants and traders of Runcorn in reference to the Manchester Ship Cellal. He had seen the plans of the scheme, and he considered that the construction of a wall in front of the Runcorn docks would create a serious interference with the trade passing to and from the estuary. and prevent its being conducted with the same facilities as at present. The promoters proposed to wall in the present deep surrounding Runcorn, and that would make a differ- ence to the extent of some eight or ten feet. The merchants and traders of Runcorn thought that in these circumstances they ought to be permitted to use the canal free of toll.— The learned counsel read one of the clauses agreed upon between the promoters and the North Staffordshire Railway Company, and asked : Would that not entirely protect your traffic ? No, it would not.—Re-examined : The only time there is for taking coasting vessels out ranged from half-an-hour to two.honrs. There would be times when it would be impossible to get vessels freer' the Runcorn dock, through the canal into the river, and it was impossible to carry on the present traffic without the option of using the ship cenal.—Mr. Ralph Hill, master mariner, Runcore, said he WAS familiar with what was proposed to be done under the Bill with respect to the making of a wall and a lock in front of the docks at Runcorn. As a practical man, know- ing how the traffic is at present worked, he asserted that it woulciebe impossible to conduct it satisfactorily if this ob- struction were created, because the outgoing and incoming vessels could not pass on the same tide. Even if the Run- corn traffic were allowed to use the canal free, a tide would in many cases be lost by the vessels which went down the canal from Runcorn.—The witness was not cross- examined. —Mr. Meysey-Thompson wished to call another witeess to the Same point, but the Earl of Milltown pointed out that the last had not been cross-examined, and the case for the Commissioners was closed.—The oppoeition of the London and North-Western Railway Company was then proceeded with.—Mr. C. Forster Clarke, manager of the Park-lane Collieries at Wigan, complained of the interference which would arise if Garston were in any shape Injured as a port. —Mr. Alfred Hevelitt, managing director of the Wigan Min- ing Compeer, gave similar evidence.—Mr. George Findlay, general manager of the London and North-Western Cam- pany, complained of the proposed interference with their line at Warrington, where the gradients would be made such that they would not be able to work their traffic either at the speed or with the conomy they now did. It would en- re. 1 a great additional cost in working the passenger traffic, becauee they would have to run an extra enginir through ; and, with regard to goods and minerals, they would have to keep sereeal additional engines at the spot at a cost of prob- ably £3,000 a year at least. On the Lancashire and Ches- hire junctions, and the Warrington and Stock') t lines there would be similar interference.% whir h would materi- ally affect the conduct of traffic, and would thus be an annoyance and detriment to trade. WEDNE'4DA.Y. At the adjourned sitting further evidence for the London and North-Western Railway Company was given by Mr. Findlay, the general manager, who said he did not believe that any appreciable portion of the coal traffic from Lanca- shire er South Yorkshire would pass over the canal. The ship canal could not compete for a tithe of Some of the traffic entering and leaving Liverpool. According to his view the Canal Company would net compete for traffic to any greater extent than 12 miles round Manchester, and they would be thereby one out of several carrying agencies. The objections to the scheme were so great, the powers asked for so enormoue, and the interests interfered with so large and numerous, that lee thought their Lordships ought not to pass the bill. He denied that the purpose of the bill in- troduced into Parliament this session by the London and North-Western Railway Company was to raise the rates for the carriage of goods. The object was to assimilate the rates authorised by several Acts of Parliament, and to settle the question of terminals.—Mr. Balfour Brown asked whether the effict of the terminal clause would not he to

raise the rates 40 per cent —Mr. Findlay said the E fhet mieffit be an addition to ihe company'e power to charge, but that did not necessarily meati an increase of rates. THURSDAY. On the Select Committee of the House of Lords resuming on Thursday its inquiry into the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, Mr. Crrierson, general manager of the Great Waseern Rail- way, was called as a witness for the London and North- Western Railway Company. He denied that i‘lanchester would become a port by the construction of the Ship Canal, and could not imagine a vessel being sent up the canal to Manchester for the same freight as to Liverpool. He doubted whether the canal would attract the Irish cattle traffic, and also whether it would have the effect of taking from Liverpool half of its cotton trade, as Mr. Adamson had I suggested. The canal would get a certain amount of traffic ; but he said emphatically that it would be a financial failure. Mr. Pope's speech for the London and North-Western Rail- way Company being reserved, the case for the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board opened, Mr. Hornby, the chairman of the Board, being the first witness. Evidence in support of the petition of the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board was then called, the first witness being Mr T. D. Hornby, chairman of the Board. He expressed his belief that if the Ship Canal were constructed, it would be a complete failure in its finaucial results, and that it would not get anything like the amount of traffic which the promoters anticipated. —Mr. W. Thorburn, of the firm of Messrs. T. Thorburn and Co., cotton brokers, said he did mot think the canal would not do away with brokerage charges, and in his opin- ion it would never yie'd a retorn.—Mr. James Beazley, managing director of the British Snipowners' Company, having been examined, the Committee adjourned.

WARRING-TON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The annual meeting of this Board was held at the Wolk- hawse on Wednesday morning. Thorn were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, Black- hurst, Jolley, Hunt, Brown, Appleton, Belharry, Ratcliffe, William Houghton, Gibson, John Houghton, Grange. Har- rison, Derbyshire, Caldwell, Forster, Swieton, Humphries, Broadbent, Owen; and J. C. eutton (clerk). ELECTION' or CHAIRMAN. The CLERK, who had been elected to the chair to conduct the preliminary huffiness, said that the first business of the meeting was to elect a chairman.—Mr. Guns:mem (the late chairman) said he had great pleasure in proposing a chair- man foe the ensuing year. As, they were aware, he had occupied the position of chairman for two years, and he thought it was quite time somebody else tools the position. They had a gentleman amongst them who, he thought, was eminently qualified for the position, and he begged to pro- pose that gentleman, who was the Rev. G. F. Roberts. (Hear, bear.) He thought they could not have a better chairman.—Mr. BLaCimuRST. in seconding the proposal, said that Mr. Roberts' experience as vice-chairman would qualify him to fill the office of chairman to the satisfaction of the Board.—Mr. JoLLEY, in supporting the proposal, referred in complimentary terms to the services of the late Chairman, but thought it would be a bad precedent to elect a chairman for three years. He had calculated that if this were done in the case of all their chairmen the youngest member of the Board would have to wait leste years for an opportunity of being chairman. (Leughtere—Messrs. Har- rison, Derbyshire, Appleton, Broadbent, Brown, and CAldwell also supported the propoeal, whieh was carried unanimously.—The Rev. G. F. RonERTS, in taking the chair, said that it was with very grateful feelings he had Listened to the very kind sentiments that had emanated from them as a body. They had .elected him to a very hoeourable position, and one which he took as a very great Compliment to himself. He should use his best efforts to prove himself to deserve their confidence and justify their choice. Of course a Board such as that like every other public body had a reputation to maintain, and be thought they should each one of them do what they could to main- tain and raise the high reputation of that Board. He remembered many years age, long before he was ever asso- ciated with that Board, and indeed hefore he came to the neighbourhood of Warrington, a gentleman, who was very competent to express such an opinion, saying to him that the Warrington Board of Gmardians were a very able body of business men. He hoped that that reputation in their hands should not be at all lessened. (Hear, hear.) Though he had possibly been more or less a silent member, he trusted he had not been a useless one. (Hear, hear.) If he might crave their indulgence he would like to throw out in the most inoffensive manner a suggestion or two as to how they might possibly conduct their business in even a more satisfactory way than they had hitherto done. It struck him in looking around that several members of that Board were business men who perhaps came there at the expense of their own interests to serve the public. Seeing that that was the case, he thought it should be their endeavour to spare the time of those gentlemea as much as Possible in their conduct of the businese. What he would deprecate was too much talking. (Hear, hear.) Purposeless talk could serve no useful end, and he would suggest that possibly the time of the gentle- men at those meetings might be to some extent at least saved if they tried to concentrate their observations as much as possible. (Hear, hear.) He also deprecated the intro- duction of anything like acrimonious feeling, because it was of the utmost importance that the business of the Board should be conducted in the most charitable feeling. They might bear in mind that if they had anything worth saying they could not strengthen it by the use of language that was not justified or by losing their temper. (Hear, hear.) At present, he added, Boards of Guaedians were kept by the Local Governmeut Board very much in leading strings, but he thought the tendency of the age was to discentralisation, and in time, he hoped, they should be thought worthy of greater confidence in common with other Boards than they had been bitbuto, (Applause). Houghton, Mr. Broadeent, and Mr. Harrison, it was carried unanimously.—Mr. JOULE? moved, and Mr. GREENING seconded a proposal that Mr. Brown be appointed junior vice-chairman.—Mr. DARETSUIRE and Mr. HARRISON hav- ing supported this proposition it was also carried unani- mously.
