div.p: RAISING THE WIND.

I pitnae doot but ye've a' heard tell o' Habbie Simpson, the piper of Kilbarchan, but I'm no thinking that ye ever heard the story that I'm pun to tell ye about him and his wife Janet. Weel, ye see, it sae happen'd, that Habbie, like mony mar noo a days, was gayan fond o' a wee dram the blue and, as the story gangs, sae was his wife; so that it gayan at ten happen'd that when Habbie yoket the fuddle, Janet, she yokel it too. Noo, it's an auld Scotch saying, and a true ane, that when a caunle is lichfet at baith ends, it sune burns dune, and it was sae verified in the present case, for Habbie waukening ane morning, after a hard fuddle, says to a Janet -

"Rise, woman, and see if ye can get me hauf a gill;. for, oh, my head is just likin' to split." "Haut a gill !" quo' Janet, "want would I get it, when there's no a' plack in a' the house, and as for takin' it on, ye ken that's clean oat o' the question,,sae ye mann just lie stilt and the best way ye can.". " Oh, Janet,' cries Erabbie again, " ye're no amiss at scheming; is there nae way, ava, ye can think o' to raise the wun.

"I'll tell ye what I'll do," quo' Janet, "I'll awa to the the laird o' Johnstone, and 11l tell him that ye're deed, and as ye're a great favourite o' his, I'm sure I'll get something frae him to help to bury ye." " Od, that'll do grand,' t quo' Habb Away gangs Janet to the laird's house, and ringing the bell, the door was opened by the lady, wha seeing Janet sae pitifu' lnkin;she says : "Keep us a' the day, is there anything wrang at hame, that ye has come here sae sun(' in the morning ?" Wrang ?" quo' Jandt, ditchin' her een wi' the tail o' her apron, " a's wrang theighter, my lady; hum our Ilabbie deed ?"

" Habbie deed ?" quo' the lady in surprise. "A weel a wat is he," quo' Janet; "an' a sair trial it is• to me, ladyfor there is no as muckle in the hoose this morn ing as wnd feed a sparrow; and whanr to get onything I'm sure I dinna ken. Oh, dear! oh, dear! that ever it should come to this o't."

" Compose yersel', Janet," quo' the lady, "and come yer wa's ben, and we's see what can be dune." Sae in gangs Janet wi' the lady, an' get a basket wi' some- biscuit and speerits, and other articles needffe for Bic an oceasion ; and thanking the lady for her kindness, comes awa hame to, Habbie fu' blithely, when doon they sat, nor did they rise till they had made an end to the contents o' the.basket. Noo, as the mill sang sings, the mair ye drink the drier ye turn, for they nae suner dune, than Rabble says r.— " Losh, Janet, that was real gold; can ye no get some mair o't I)"
" Na, na," quo' Janet, "1 hae played ma part ; it's your turn noo."

" Oh, very weal," quo' Ilabbie, " If it's my turn noo ye main just be deed next." "01, 1 hae nae objections," quo' she, "sae away ye gang, and let's see what ye can do." Weel, awa gangs Ilabbie, and meeting the laird just coming hams frae a hunting party, he says— This is a fine day, laird." _ .

"A flue day, Ilibbfe,' quo' the laird: " boo is a' wi' ye ? Are ye no coming up to play us a spring on the pipes the nicht ?" "It wadna leuk wed, laird, for me to be seen playing on the pipes at your house, and my am n wife lying a corpse at hame." "What! is Janet deed!" quo' -the laird. „ .. . . .

" Atweel is she," quo' Ilabbie ; "and I'm sum it couldna has happent on a waur time' fez there's neither meat Nor sifler in the house; and hoo to get her decently aneath the yird l'm sure I dinna ken." "Dinna vex yersel' about That," quo' tha.laird, giving him some money ; "there is a tri:le for you, in the meantime, and come up to the house by and by, and I shall see what can be done for you." . . .

Habbie thanked thehird for his kindness, bade hiai good day, and cam' away home, gayan weel pleased wi' what he had gotten, and Sell'S Janet out wi, the bottle for rnair whisky to carry on the spree. In the meantime, hams gangs the laird, whaur the first thing that he heard was, that Mb- hie Simpson was deed. 'Na, na," quo' he, "it's no Babble; it's only Janet." " It's Habbie," quo' the lady; wasna Janet here this morning, hersel', and telt me? and didna she get awa some

THE ALLEGED MURDER AND SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS. On Friday evening, Mr S Brighouse, coroner, held an in- quest on the bodies of Jane Hamilton, forty-three years of age, and Thomas Hamilton, four years of age, wife and son of James Hamilton, a labourer, 23, nightield-st., Sutton. Having given evidence of identification, Hamilton was questioned by the coroner. In reply, he said he last saw the deceased alive about half-past five on Thursday morn- ing. His wife was awake, and his son was asleep when he went to work. Early in the afternoon they were brought home dead. He had not noticed anything peculiar about his wife recently, nor had she done anything that would lead him to think she would take away her own life. Some things had troubled her a little. She had not had too much money to buy things she would have liked, and she had grumbled. Witness used to get better wages than he did now. Mrs. Alice Marsh, who lives at Sutton Leach, said that about eleven o'clock on Thursday morning she saw the de- ceased and her son in Mill-lane going in the direction of the dam in which she was found. She was then 200 yards off. Witness went to a shop, and on returning saw an object leaning over the bridge, but did net then know it was Mrs. Hamilton. All at once the object disappeared, and a Mrs. Smith beckoned to witness to come back, saying she heard a child scream. She looked over the bridge and saw a body in, and then raised an alarm. She noticed nothing strange In deceased when she met her. Mrs. Smith, whose residence is in close proximity to the bridge in question, said she was sitting in her front room upstairs and heard a child scream. She looked through the window, but could not see anyone, and the thought struck her that perhaps a child might be in the water. She ran out and looked over the railing of the bridge, and saw a little hat on the water, and what she thought was the form of a child drifting under the bridge. Mrs. Hamilton mnst also have been under the bridge, as she saw her nowhere about. Mr. Barlow and Mr. Redmond came and got the bodies oat. An Irishman came down the lane, and got into the water up to his knee. He then screamed, and they bad to drag him out.—The Coroner: In the absence of any direct proof we want to get at the most feasible theory. Pos- sibly the child might have gone through and the woman gone after it.—Witness: I did not see the child go in. I could not see how it occurred. Jane Norman, an elderly person who lives two doors away from the Hamiltms, said she saw the deceased go out about half-past ten o'clock that morning holding the little boy's hand. She had no conversation with her then. Deceased bad three more children. She wae a very high-minded woman, and wanted to get on faster than she could. Wit- ness had heard her say she could not face her debts, and on one occasion she named a place in St. Helens that she did not like to pass She said she was frightmed of Friday coming. Th,mas Michael Barlow 'gave corroborative eviderve.— In reply to a juryman, Inspector Keighley said the water was three feet deep. rolice Constable Mather said the child was a cripple, and when the maker went out she always took it by the hand The Coroner said the evidence waolrefere the jury. Lie could only say that upon the evidence before them he con- sidered their best course was to find an open verdict. It had been suggested that this woman, whilst in an unsound state of mind, had murdered her child and committed suicide The bridge, it had been stated, was of a dangerous construction, and it was quite as feasible to pat forward the theory that the child had fallen in, and the mother, in her anxiety to save it, had also got into the water, as to say it was murder and suicide. His (the coroner's) own opinion was that it woold be very cruel indeed to the relatives of the deceased on that evidence to say that she had murdered her child and then committed suicide. The jury returned an open verdict, adding a rider that they considered the bridge was in a dangerous state.

On Wednesday evening the annual meeting of the Grand Lodge of English Masons was held at Freemasons' Hall. The Grand Master's chair was taken, in the absence of the Prince of Wales, by the Earl Gf Lathom. The Prince was declared to have been reinstalled as Grand Master of the Order.

Collections were made on Sunday to pay off the balance of the debt of £7,000. They were found guilty of wounding with in- tent to do grievious bodily harm, and sentenced to five yeirs' penal servitude. PRESCOT.

THE SUPPORT OF A FATHER AND MOTHER.—At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, an order was made upon James Killelea, a labourer at Widnes, to contribute 2s per week towards the support of his father and mother, who are at present chargeable to the Prescot Union. TRESPASSING AT KNOWSLEY. James Schofield and Edward Connolly, strangers to the neighbourhood, were charged at the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, with trespassing in pursuit of game on land at Knowsley, in the occupation of Robert Gillons.—Mr. S. Marsh, solicitor, ap- peared to prosecute, and the prisoners, who pleaded guilty, were each fined 20s and costs or one month's iinpriBon- ment.

Boman or GUARDIANS.—The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Whiston,- en Thursday forenoon. The Workhouse Master's report stated there were 431 inmates this week+against 442 last week, and 437 in the corresponding week of last year. Fifty-three vagrants had been relieved during the week, against 54 in the correspond- ing week last year, and 174 boys and girls were chargeable to the Union. The election of an assistant overseer for the township 6f Eccleston in the place of Mr. Dunn, wbo had been called upon to resign, then took place. From the ap- plicants for the vacant post five candidates were selected to appear before the Board, namely, Thomas Parkinson reliev- ing officer,. Prescot ; Fred. Fidler, clerk, Th:gsmore . . .

House, Eccleston ; Edward Pennington, clerk, 58, Owen- street, Thatto Reath; William Robinson, clerk, Windie Smithies; and John Tyrer, farmer, Catchdalo Moss. Twenty-six Guardians voted, 15 being in favour, of Mr. Parkinson, who was declared elected, seven in favour of Mr. Robinson, and four in favour of Mr. Tyrer. Mr. William Bullock, relieving officer for the Parr and Sutton district, will be transferred to Prescot, and a relieving officer for Parr and Sutton at a salary of £lOO per annum will be ad- vertised for.

A PILESCOT RUFFIAN DESERVEDLY PUNISIIED.—Before Mr. W. L. Evans and A. R. Gladstone, at the Prescor Petty Sessions on Tuesday, Joseph Ho!croft, a strong-looking young fellow, was charged, on remand, with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Middlebrook—P.C. Mid- dlebrook stated that on the afternoon of the 21st April he saw a large crowd of people at the corn:r of St. Helens. road, Preemie. The prisoner was drunk, and his face was bleeding as if he had been fiAhting. When he went up to the prisoner the latter began to curse and swear, and struck him several times on the chest, and kicked him in the stomach with his foot. With the assistance of other con- stables the prisoner was sec3red and locked up. He was very violent all the way to the office, and had to be dragged part of the way.—Superintendent Barker stated the pri- soner had been several times previously convicted for as- saulte on the police. He was a great annoyance to the inhabitants of Prescot by his disorderly coniuct.—The Chairman said there were convictions against the prisoner for violence every year since 1674. He asked what was the eztreme penalty.—The Clerk: £2O, or six months.—The Chairman (to the prisoner): You will havi to go to gaol for three minim with brad labour without the option of a fine.

CAtimos To Commti—Before Messrs. W. Blinkhorn and A. B. Gladstone at the Prescot Tatty Sessions, on Tues- day, George Brooks, of Truest, a collier employed at the Cares Colliery;Whiston,was summoned for committing a breach of one of the special rules in force at that colliery, The defendant pleaded guilty."-Mr. J. 0. ,Swift, of St. Helens, appeared for the complainant. lie said that on the 9th April when Mr. Barton, the manager of the mine, was going on his rounds he found the defendant and his " mate " preparing for a shot to , bring dawn the coal. They had made a hollow under the coal and the defendant was lying beneath the coal without it being in any way supported by sprags or props. Mr. Barton spoke to the defendant about the danger he was in,•and the defendant replied that it did not matter and he thought the coal was safe after "sound- ing " it. He Baird Mr. Bartma to look over It. Mr. Swift added that one of the rules of the mine was that all miners should secure the roofs and sides of their working places with props and sprags. About five weeks ago at that col- liery two men were seriously injured by failing to comply with the rule, which had been framed for the protection of the workmen.—Mr. George Barton, the certificated manager, then gave eyidence to the ft reg )ing effect.-The Bench said the rules were for the safety of the men and they n3ust be observed. div.head: etters to the (Editor.
div.p: etters to the (Editor.

THE POLICE AND THE IRISH. cannot help feeling curious as to how the police of Warrington intend to justify their recent treatment of the Irishmen of this town. Do they suspect that Warring- ton, of all places, is the centre of a malevolent m nspiracy, or have they been /stimulated into preternatural activity by the dynamite shocks of the last twelve months or so? If the former be the cause, they certainly cannot be compli- mented on their methods of unravelling the plot, and if it be the latter it would seem that a Wairington policeman's nerves are not affected by such shocks till a few months after thosa of other people. If they think that after forcing themselves as unwelcome intruders into a company of Irish- men these selfsame Irishmen are going to sit down and hatch a treasonable plot for the special purpose of being sent to penal servitude, it seems to me to prove a simplicity on the part of the polic9 that is not of this world. Men who are so supremely innocent of the wiles and strategems of evil-doers, and conspirators above all others, are clearly ripe ' for translation to some better world. At all events they have clearly mistaken their vocation, and the least that can ho done, if there be any desire to keep from pollution such rare au I refreshing iznocence, is to translate them from a police force. And as to the dynamite explosions, the more the evidence that is got with regard to them the more does it tend to clear the Irishmen who live in England of any participation in these crimes. The English-Irishmen, if they may be so called, who have been arrested in connec- tion with these explosions, seem only to have been arrested in order to be let loose again. Then why in the name of all that is fair and prudent should the Warrington Irishmen be subjected to such irritating and humiliating treatment? In- stead of leading to the detection of crime, it seems to me to be little short of an incentive to it. A good deal that is very obvious might be said upon this subj•ct from a higher standpoint. It is an acknowledged calamity that Irishmen should feel so bitter and hostile to this country, and a good deal has been done lately to remove this feeling, but it may be taken for granted that neither the efforts-of statesmen nor of princes will be of any avail if the Irishmen in Eng- lish towns are to be treated as aliens, and subjected, like ticket-of.leave men, to the petty inquisitions of prejudiced policemen.—' am, sir, A SAXON. THE WARRINGTON LIBEL CASE. Sir,—The fact of the grand jury at Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday igmoing the bill in the case against Mr. Grice, of having libelled Mr. Speakman in your columns, and the verdict of the jury in the Whitehaven slander case, appear to me to show the current of public feeling on these mat- ters. We have heard so much of damages that have been awarded to plaintiffs in cases which have of themselves been extremely trivial, that it is pleasing to find that there is some Limit to this sort 0 thing. I think that a man who maliciously slanders another is deserving of punishment, and severe punishment, but unfortunately there are people only too willing to take advantage of what opportunity the law allows to be avenged of some petty slight or imagined insult, and not from an honest desire to clear a sullied char- acter. It required a very biassed mind to discover any sug- gestion of lib-I in the letter signed "Anti-Humbug" that appeared in The Examiner, and which formed the subject of the Warrington Libel Case" which has so exercised the feelings of certain political sections in the town. Per- haps the grand jury, composed of gentlemen of intelligence and learning, in not allowing the cases to go for trial, will have somewhat opened the eyes of local jus- tices of the peace, and of others who seemed to dis- cover an enormity in what to common-sense judg- ment appeared to he a reasonable cornplaint. The " Lae Whitehaven slander case " that went before the judge and jury was also extremely trivial, a White- haven spirit merchant having merely spoken of another person in the trade as a " shabby fellow," and as being " barely honest." For this the "injured one " desired compensation, and didn't get it. A few more similar de- cisions would perhaps teach combative people the folly of occupying the time of a judge and jury in hearing, and thus making more public, imaginary grievances. To me it seems that it should not be difficult to discriminate between foul slander, calculated and intended to inflict injury, and an injudicious remark made in a passion, or an honest attempt to redress irregularities in an Institution provided for a cer- tain:political party.—Yours &e. ANOTHER "ANTI-HUMBUG."

May 1,1885. PRIMOGENITURE AND THE LAND LAWS. Sir,—From a passage in one of the heathen poets a recent writer has lately inferred that an eldest eon who refused to divide the inheritance fairly with his younger brothers and sisters must have fared badly in Tartarus, according to the doctrines of the ancients, if the house of correction to which Rhadamanthus, the heathen judge of hell (who must have been a most awful old fellow), consigned the offenders who came before him, be correctly described by Virgil. In England primogeniture seems to have been first established by custom and not by statute law, and to have been modified from time to time, according to the public needs. From this our reformers have come to the conclusion that it may be changed and improved again so as to bring the land laws into accord with the public necessities of the present day. The following remarks will explain my meaning : 'the right of primogeniture in males seems anciently to have prevailed only among the Jews. The first-born in the patriarchal times had a superiority over his brethren and, in the absence of the father, was the priest of the family. Among the Jews he had a double portion of the inheritance; in the fame manner as, by the laws of Henry I. of England, the eldest son had the capital fee of his father's possessions, and no other pre-eminence; and as the eldest daughter bad the principal mansion when the estate descended in co- parcenary. What Gibbon calls "The insolent law of primo- geniture ' bad no place among the ancient humane; the two sexes were placed on a just level ; all the sons and all the daughters were entitled to an equal portion of the metre. menial estate. The Greeks, the Britons, the Saxons, the Danes, divided the lands equally among all the children at large, and some among the males only. The equal division of the patrimonel estate among all the children at large, i.e., in the same way in some respects as a man's leasehold and personal estate is divided under the statutes for distri- buting the property of intestates among his next of kin, is certainly the most equitable and natural way. Before the conquest the descent of lands was to all the sons alike. Socage estates frequently descended to all the sons equally, till the time of Henry lit., when in imitation of lands in ckivalry, they had almost entirely fallen into the right of aucceesion by primogeniture, except in the county of Kent, where they gloried in the preservation of their ancient tenure by which land became the joint inheritance of all the sons ; and except in some other particular places, where special modes of descent prevailed. The right of primogeniture which calls the eldest-born to the crown was not introduced into France until compara- tively very late. It was unknown to the first and see led races of kings. The four aqua of Clovis shared the kingdom equally among themselves. The song of Louis Is Debonnaire did the same. When Hugh Capet ascended the throne, the prerogative of succession to the crown was appropriated to the first-born. But this is a special subject, in favour of which a good deal may be said, and which is not now in question. It is a remarkable fact that although primogeniture gene- rally prevails, yet there are several other modes in which land descends in the United Kingdom. Now the question -at present seems to be whether an Act should not be paned to simplify and improve the descent and devolution of real to property and to make the same uniform in every part of Great Britain and Ireland.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, T. FRODSOM. 27th April, 1885. N. 8.-1 have not seen the new bill to enfranchise copy' holds, but as I understand it is made up of above 50 clauses, lam afraid it will not be good for much. By the Statute of Charles 11. feudal tenures were abolished (except copy- holds). Would it not have been a shorter and better plan to have repealed this exception and to have declared that all the lands in the kingdom should henceforth be deemed and be fee simple freeholde, subject, of course, to the quit rents and heriots to which the same are now subject; just as land at Manchester is conveyed in fee simple, subject to a perpetual chief rent. T. F. THE IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. Sir,—Sitting down to pen the following few lines, I feel how all-important is the subject, and how deeply necessary it is for a persuasive and a loving friend to speak to the Irish. I attended their meeting on Sunday afternooon lest at Warrington; I listened to their speakers with atten- tion, and to what conclusion could I come respecting the hazy programme hinted at by the speakers? Just this, that once more were the Irish people forging shackles wherewith to bind themselves. Is it enough for the Irish people to assemble in their thousands, and in mad outbursts of passion to cry out their hatred of England and Deg- land's people? Is it enough for their speakers to declaim against " Buckshot Forster," or to consign the Lord-Lieu- tenant of Ireland, Earl Spencer, to the hands of the public executioner as a murderer ? I should surely think not ; these are but the ravings of impotency, and what avails the wild and unseemly language against Dublin Castle ? Nothing ; 'tie mere battling with the wind. But then, our Irish friends have an object in view. They also have learnt that organization is necessary, if good re- sults are to be attained. These results are, Charles Stuart Parnell to be crowned on College Green, and Irishmen to make laws for the Irish people. And so our Irish brethren would knock down "the blood-purpled robes of English Royalty" simply to transplant a rotten branch to Ireland. I would ark Irishmen if it is not clear that the tendency of the age is to root out, root and branch, everything that tends towards keeping the peoples of the world asunder? Yet, here they would set up another crowned master and fall down and worship him. They cheer to the echo the wildest sentiment ever uttered by man, never giving a thought to the dire necessity that ex'sts for complete and friendly understanding between English and Irish workmen. Suppose for a moment they could set up C. S. Parnell as a Ring in Ireland. 'What then ? Where is their armv and navy to be got from to guarantee them an independ- ence? Is there no inward Toice telling them that after they have once severed the tie which connects them with England they would, like the Kilkenny cats, at once set to aid destroy themselves ? This is no vain prophecy. One of their speakers in elequent language drew a vivid picture of the doings of Irish patriots in the past. Some of their jecte were gained, but only in the slme sense that reform' hg measures were passed for the whole of the Kingdom. Mr. Eiggar tells them that Protestant Ulster will in the future work for die-union alorg with the other three provinces. This is fain,. The Lord BC29IIIOtEB of Ireland are not vet an extinct treed, and he knows it. He kipws more than this; he knows that slaculd the Irish leaders issue a maul-

1 festo instructing Lisle voters how to vote it will be the I signal for the English parties to coalesce and throw to the \winds the whole of the Irish political chicanery. What! Do Irishmen think English Radicals will quietly stand by while, to use the chairman's words, "they close their eyes as to the candidate, and simply vote according to instructions." Mr. Biggar says neither political party must have a big majority, and then it will ' b 3 possible far the Irish leaders to make bargains with Whig or Tory as the case may be. English politics, Eng- lish necessities, are to be thrown to the winds so that they may carry on their everlasting brawls. The answer is : " There is one way out of this; give us our independence." What if we did this. Would Irishmen clear out of Eng- land? Could they persuade the chairman, whose "interests In %Varrington are as great as Mr. Hunt's," to pack off bag and baggage to Ireland ? Not a bit of it. Would the Irish working-men I saw at the meeting, well dressed and respect- able looking, differing in no wise from the" hated English" —woield these, I say, leave their prosperous situations and his them to their barren mountains? Not a single Irish- man would he found with sufficient self-abnegation to com- mit so suicidal an act. No ; our interests as English and Irish workmen are identical. If we pull together our suc- cess is certain ; if, like the bundle of sticks, we are taken sepa:ate, then we shall continue to toil for— The grasping traders—who for gold Grind sinew, blood, and bone— Oppress the feeble, and the old, And scorn the pauper's groan • They share the fair and fruitful' lands With lords of noble birth, And honest labour's horny hands For them must till the earth i Now, Mr. Editor, why do I write in this strain ? It is because I, as a Radical, feel sure they are committing a grave mistake, and this in a many ways. I listened anxiously to Mr. Biggar for a condemning word against the outrages Englishmen have recently been subjected to. Not a word of condemnation was uttered. Perhaps leading Irish- men think it would be unwise to take home to themselves the crimes recently committed in London. Mr. A. M. Sul- livan did not think so when he published his manly and honourable appeal of February 24, 1883. Nor do sympa- thising Englishmen think so, and I venture to throw out a word of warning, that unless some other mode of warfare is I adopted a fearful reckoning day is not far distant. I cannot I see why the Irish do not adopt a wider and more compre- hensive method of marshalling forces together for the I redress of grievances. The sinks in and about Dublin Castle ' certainly want disinfecting, but English Radicals .vorking [ with Irishmen could eff,ct this reform in a much more speedy way than the exclusively Irish system now adopted. But then English Radicalism does not include Die-union; it 1, rather means the welding together of international bonds, I working for the freedom of the people, and so to "consolidate that co-operation which renders irresistible a community"— working for a common object. lam sure the few English- men present at Vie meeting of the Irish League must have, like myself, heard the cold cynical words of Mr. Biggar, when referring to Russia's march towards India, with some- thing like contempt and disgust for the man who could so degrade himself. Do Irishmen think nothing of their kith and kin who form so large a portion of the British army ? Is the rule of Russia so much more beneficial than that of England that they would be pleased to see it established in India? And yet, in a cold callous fashion, they could burst oat in laughter when brutal reference was made to Russia striding towards India. Let Irishmen protest as strongly as may be against Chief Constable Hunt and his alleged at- tempt to coerce employers into action against Irish work- men; but let them remember this, that while they are fight- ing for freedom they neglect no opportunity of coercing others who differ from them. Not only in St. Stephens do they de their best to rob other men of their liberty, but here in Warrington, whenever occ ision offers itself, they become blgoted intolerants, and would rob the platform of its liberty, and the mind of its freedom. Their chairman, referring to Mr. Mc- Minnies, said he was sorry he was going to retire, as it would deprive Irishmen of the opportunity of voting against him. One opportunity had been neglected by our respec- ted member, whereby a service could have been rendered to Ireland, and this was enough to condemn him in the eyes et Irishmen. On thia point I challenge the speaker to make good his WOITIP. I also challenge him to prove the in- creased benefits his countrymen would receive by voting for a Tory. Let Irishmen throw their meetings open, invite English thought, co-operate with Englishmen, and let all their actions be fearless ant above board, and then they may win success. CLIFFORD DIX. April 2704 1885. .

div.head: ALLEGED LIBEL AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE ALLEGED LIBEL AT WAR- RINGTON.

----•- -- At the Liverpool Spring Assizes on Wednesday the grand jury threw out the bill in the case against Joseph Grice, of Warrington, who was indicted on the commitment of Warrington Borough Magis- trates "for having, at Warrington, on the 3f st January, unlawfully published a certain defamatory libel of and concerning one Thomas Orrell Speak- man." The alleged libel appeared in a letter (bearing date January 26th, igBs, and the signature of "Anti-Humbug,"l which was published in the correspcndence columns of this journal. It re- ferred to the new Conservative Club in Sankey- street, of which Mr. Speakman is manager, and dealt with the manner in which the club was attended to, making several complaints regarding certain irregularities, and appealing to the club committee to rectify matters. Mr. Grice, the writer, who was a member of the club when the letter was written, had been out on bail since his committal by the magistrates. He was from the first confident that there was no case against him, and refused to enter. tam any proposal that he should apologise and pay costs. The result justifies his judgment and shows the folly of the prosecution.

A WARRINGTON PUB LICAN KILLED ON THE RAILWAY. A. sad accident occurred near Arpley Station, War- rington, on the London and North-Western railway line, on Thursday evening, by which Mr. Thomas Brooks, beerhouse keeper, of the Ring-o'-Bells Inn, Wilderspool-road, Warrington, was instantaneously killed. Mr. Brooks, who was 78 years old, having been to Liverpool, had just got back home, and, as was usual with him, was walking up the line in the direction of his house on Wilderspol-road—about too yards distant—when the train by which he had come from Liverpool came up behind him as it was starting to pursue its journey. Deceased was then about 20 yards from the crossing gates, and was walking in the six foot. He stepped into the four foot to avoid the train, and in doing so placed himself directly in front of another train that was coming from Manchester. A man named John Woods, seeing the danger to Mr. Brooks, shouted to him, and the driver of the train, William Whalley. put the whistle on at full. Deceased, however, apparently did not hear the warnings nor see the train, and was knocked down, being struck by the buffer. Ile was thrown a distance of about six yards, his head was cut open at the back, and he was otherwise badly injured. He would not be above seven or eight yards from the train when he stepped in front of it, and the spot where the accident occurred is but a short distance from where the , deceased resided.

ALLEGED ATTEMPTED CHILD MURDER AT WARRINGTON. A single young 'woman named Agnes Mairs, 26 years of age, who has for the past .six months been engaged as laundress at the Warrington Infectious Diseases Hospital, bas been removed in custody to the Workhouse, on suspicion of haying committed a grave offence. A little after two o'clock on Wednesday after- noon one of the servants employed at the Institu- tion in question heard a cry, apparently that of a child, proceeding from inside a tin box baonging to Mairs, and she reported what she had heard to the matron, Mrs. Jones. That lady then went to Mairs and asked that she should be allowed to look into the bo-x, which was locked. At first Mairs was disinclined to consent and protested, but Mrs. Jones insisting she ultimately allowed the box to be searched. In it was found an infant, a few hours old, which was alive and healthy, the fact of there being a small slit in the box having assisted respiration, and no doubt saved the child's life. The police authorities were informed of the matter, and Mairs was subsequently placed in custody. We un- derstand that she will be charged with attempting to murder her child. It is possible that the case may resolve itself into one of attempt to conceal the birth of the child. Mairs went to the hospital with an excellent character from previous employers, and during her engagement there conducted herself with propriety, and was a hard-working servant. Her condition had been so carefully concealed that it was not suspected that she was enceinte

div.p: SACRED CONCEKT AT WARRINGTON. On Wednesday evening Farmer's well-known or- atorio "Christ and His Soldiers " was given in the Bold-street Wesleyan Schools, in the presence of a good audience. The performers numbered about one hundred, consisting of a full band and chorus of members of the Warrington Orchestral -Union. The solos were entrusted to Miss Isabel Monks (con- tralto). Miss Riley (soprano), Mr. F. J. Dell (tenor), and Mr. W. H. Wallington (bass) ; and the whole were under the efficient conductorship of -Mr. C. H. Pigot. Although this oratorio was mainly intended by its composer to be sung to children and young persons, it has become a favourite amongst both young and old who have any taste for simple sacred song, and when adequately rendered there are few of the more famous compositions of the great mas- ters which better win the appreciation of an ordinary audience. On Wednesday evening all the parts, and more especially perhaps the solos, were very successfully represented. The first solo, "Hark, the glad sound, the Saviour comes," was taken by Miss Riley, and the easy and graceful manner in w bleb she acquitted herself won considerable applause. The singularly sweet and pleasing carol commenc- ing " In the field with their flocks abiding" was rendered by the choir and band with notable har- mony and precision, and was indeed one of the best performances of the evening. The chorus "Oh, come all ye faithful" WU well executed, and warmly applauded. Mr. W. H. Walling. ton's enterpretation Of the song " And did the sons of God appear" was somewhat lacking in expression, but he was handicapped by the lather defective accompaniment. The chorus "Ride on, ride on in majesty" having been very creditably dealt with, the chorale " Tbe night of agony bath passed " viltss essayed, but its effect was undoubtedly marred by the discordancy which crept in amongst , 1 the instruments. In the sole " When I survey the . wondrous cross" Mr. F. J. ball scored a success, be- ing applauded until he had bowed his acknowledg. ments. The solo "By Jesus grave on either hand" brought out Miss Monk's fine vocal qualities; she was recalled and repeated the latter part of the piece Miss Riley re-appeared as a soloist in the solo and chorus "Jesus Christ is risen to•day " and the song " Our bleat Redeemer ere He breathed," in both of which she won the loudly expressed encomiums of the audience. In the second part Miss Riley again took the first solo, " Hark a thrilling voice is sounding," after which Mr. Wallington was vary successful in the solo and chorus "In token that thou shalt not fear," and was loudly applauded. Mr. Dell appeared at his best in the solo " The Son of God goes forth to war," which he dealt with in the most effective and expressive style. He was recalled and repeated a few verses. Another chorus, by the rendering of which the whole company won the admiration of the audience, was that com- mencing " Soldiers of Christ arise." Mr. Walling- ton having effectively taken two more solo parts, Miss Monks evoked quite an outburst of acclama- tion by her very expressive rendering of the solo "Rock of ages," and the applause was renewed on her repetition of the passage. In the remaining portion of the programme the most notable item was I a quartet, " Jima died for us and rose again," by I Misses Monks and Riley, and Messrs. Wallington and Dell, which was encored. The concert on the whole was a success, and the manner in which it was carried out was such as to win many good opinions for the 1 Orchestral Union.

ASSMILT ON A DARESTSIIRY LABOURER —Martain Higgins, a farm labourer employed at Daresbury, was taken to War- rington Hsspital on Sunday night, soff-qing from a wound on the head, which was attended to by Dr. Richmond. The injured man was in Bank-street when another man, at pre- sent unknown, attacked him, and, striking him a severe blow on the head, knocked him down.

div.head: EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 2, 1885. I A SANKEY CASE AT LIVERPOOL ! LATEST NEWS.
div.p: THE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, MAY 2, 1885. I A SANKEY CASE AT LIVERPOOL ! LATEST NEWS.

ASSIZES. At Liverpool Assizes on Thursday, a case was heard in which William Kerfoot, farmer, residing at Sankey, near Warrington, was the plaintiff, and sought to recover dam- ages for wrongful distress from Michael Hughes, a land- owner. Mr. Addison, Q.C., and Mr. Pickford (instructed by Mr. Jenkins, solicitor, Warrington,) were counsel for the plaintiff, and Mr. Charles Russell, QC., M.P., and Mr. Walton (instructed by Messrs. Forsbaly and Hawkins, solicitors, Liverpool,) for the defendant. The plaintiff had occupied the Kerfoot Farm, Sankey, belonging to the de- fendant, for neatly 30 years. his rental up to 1874 being £l5B a year, and afterwards it was raised to £l9O. A few days before the last rent audit, in December, a distress was put in for £313 for rent, but the bailiff was sulmequently withdrawn temporarily, possession being finally taken on behalf of the defendant early in January, and the farm stock and produce, which the plaintiff valued at nearly £6OO, being sold to meet the reduced claim of £303 The sale realised £354, and after the expenses had been allowed for there remained a balance to the plaintiff's credit of £l5. The defendant's agent. Mr. Longton, stated in cross-exami- nation that he put in the distress because he had heard from his brother-in-law, who occupied an adjoining farm, that the bailiffs were in possession of the plaintiff's farm, and were removing his stock, which was not true. For the de- fence, it was contended that the amount distrained for was due, and the distress was perfectly regular. 'l'6e evidence as to the settlements for rent between the plaintiff and the defendant's agent was of a conflicting nature, and the main point at issue in the case was whether a sum of £9O had been paid, as alleged by the plaintiff, in respect of rent for the year 1380, which the defendant denied.—The jury found for the plaintiff,damages £175. His lordship granted costs.

The mother of the murdered girl has since become quite demented, and has had to be placed under re- straint. She has also given premature birth to a child.

div.head: WARRINGTON RADICAL CLUB.
div.p: WARRINGTON RADICAL CLUB.

The weekly meeting of the mmbers of the Warrington Radical Club took place on Saturday evening, at the Club- room, Sankey-street. On the conclusion of the ordinary business, a paper on "Socialism" was read by Mr. W. H. Chapman before an excellent attendance of members and visitors. Mr. Chapman commenced by observing that the limited time at his disposal would not permit of anything like an exhaustive treatment of the steadily-growing prin- ciples of social and Political life referred to in his paper, but he would briefly submit to the meeting the framework, as it were, of the subject. He stated that Socialism aimed at the regeneration of society by substituting association in place of competition, and sought to secure a more equal distribution of wealth among the masses. He contended that Socialists regarded the human race 83 one family or brotherhood, and therefore claimed the earth as the heritage of the race, and not the property of the few. He stated that land, light, air, and water were the free gifts of nature to all mankind, and any law, or custom of society, that allowed any person to monopolise these gifts to the detriment of the rights of others, was to be condemned, and ought to be abolished. Socialism claimed equal rights for all, and equal duties from all. It claimed the duty of all able-bodied adults to perform some useful work, either brain work or hand work, and the right of each to the full fruits of his labour. Education in all its branches should be con.

ferred upon every member of the state free, in order that each one should enter upon manhood and womanhood fully trained and prepared to perform the duties devolving upon them as members of society. Land, light, air, and water being claimed as the common property of the people, as the State, involved their right also, to fall control over the production and distribution of all material wealth; conse- quently monopoly would cease to exert its banejul influ- ence. He claimed that under highly developed Socialistic conditioas, labour of all kinds would be rendered agree- able, and drudgery come to an end, because every person would have ample opportunity to select such occupation as each was beat fitted for by nature and training. The hours of labour would be much reduced, thus allowing plenty of leisure time for recreation and improvement. The aged, the infirm, and the young would all be provided for out of the common fund of the State, and thus charity (so called) and pauper relief would have no place in Socialism. Class and court distinction would Ise unknown; the only classes recognised would be men, women, and children. Tbe watch- words of Socialists were Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity; and it was contended that under the beneficent reign of Socialism peace and concord would supplant war and die- cord.—A most interesting discussion then arose, the pro- ceedings concluding with a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Chapman for his paper. An adjournment of the weekly meetings over the summer recess to the first Saturday in September next was agreed to.

div.head: WESLEYAN LOCAL PREACHERS
div.p: WESLEYAN LOCAL PREACHERS

ASSOCIATION. On Thursday evening a meeting was held in Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington, in connection with the Wes- leyan Local Preachers' Matual Aid Association. The chair was occupied by Mr. J. Moon, of Liverpool, who was sup- ported by the Revs. J. McTurk, G. E. Cutting, and J. H. Jones ; Messrs. R. Garnett, E.. J. Guest, J.P., R. Cook. E. Brown (Lymm), Barlow, J. Hayward, R Ford (ben. sec.), and Silcock (Moore.) There was a good attendance. There was also present an efficient orchestral band, under the conductorship of Mr. R. H. Pearson, which accompanied the singing of several old Methodist tunes. A prayer hav- ing been offered up by Mr. Brown, the CECALRMAIS who was received with applause, said he could assure them that be felt extreme pleasure in occupying the chair that evening, from the fact that their assembling together was in connec- tion with what all of them most be deeply interested in, that was in connection with the Local Preachers' Mutual Aid Association. (Applause.) The association had a two- fold object in view. The first was to relieve Local preachers when sick and in need. He had always felt a very deep interest in that institution, and there was no class of men in connection with the Wesleyan body more deserving, and who merited their sympathy more than the local preachers. (Hear, hear.) It was true that their travelling preachers were men of talent and ability, and men who had as much aptitude for commercial life as the best and cleverest men in the commercial world, but who had spent their youth in preparing for future work in connection with the church of Christ, while if they only studied their own and their family's pecuniary interests they could do themselves a thousand times more good than they ever succeeded in doing by oc- cupying a Methodist pulpit. They were, how- ever, men specially called to fill the pulpit ; but the local preachers were men who -turned out as early as any one to work bard for their livelihood and for the maintenance of their families, and most of them did not leave servants at home to wait upon their wives and fami- lies. Yet it used to be 30 or 40 years ago that the local preacher woull have twelve or thirteen Sundays out of the quarter to walk long distancesand preach the gospel, and re- turn home is the evening tired and worn out. It was a grand werk that they did, and as long as he lived he would help them. (Applause.)—Mr. FORD, the hon. sec, of the local branch of the Association, submitted a report from which it appeared that it had on its books 2,963 members and 930 hon. members. The total income during the past year was £2,420 Oa 31. Of the benefit dispensed War- riogton circuit had received X 33 2364, which was £l9 lls more than had been subscribed by the circuit. There were 13 members of the association in this circuit and one hon. member.—The Rev. J. Mc furor, in the course of an address, said the great religious work in this country represmted by Methodism had very largely been carried forward by the assistance of those who werb termed local preachers. To- day they had an army of well nigh fifteen thousand local preachers, who were carrying on a vast work which they all admired. (Applause.)—Mr. R. CI...AR- NE IT thOUght the objects of the Association only needed to be thoroughly known in order to win the support of all their friends.—Mr. E. J. Guest referred to the arduous duties which the local preachers undertook, and he said it was a great pity that they were receiving more in that cir- cuit than they gave. (Hear, hear.)—Suitable addresses were also oiven' by Mr. Hayward, Mr. Brown, the Rey. G. E. Cuttin, Mr. R. Cook, Mr. IV. Y. Lawton, and the 11-3 y. J. H. Jones.—On the motion of Mr. BARLOW, seconded by Mr. FORD, a veto of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, who in responding promised an annual subscription of ten Pounds.—On the motioh of Mr. Str.cocK, seconded by Mr. ROYLANCR, a vote of thanks was accorded the orchestra It was announcel that the total subscriptions that evening amounted to £25 Os 4.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.

PURCHASE oF THE BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION. At the inquiry before the Select Committee, on Friday, Mr. Pember announced that the promoters had arranged terms with the Bridgewater Canal Company for the pur- chase of the Bridgewater Canal and the Mersey and Irwell Navigation. The arrangement was that the promoters should within two years of the passing of the bill, pur- chase both undertakings for the sum of £1,710,000, or the promoters should, within two months of the passing of the bill, deposit in the Bank of England £20,000 as security for the completion of the purchase. Further evidence was then celled for the Mersey Dock Board, and the committee ad. journed.:

div.head: GREEK MENISIRY.
div.p: THE GREEK MENISIRY.

The Central News Athens Correipindent telegraphs :—A new Ministry has been formed as follows: M. Delynis (pre- mier), finance and foreign affairs ; M. Avromihales, war; M. Papamihalopulo, the interior; M. Antonopoulos, justice; M. Zigomals, religion, and M. Romas, marine. THE SUEZ CANAL CONIMISSION.

PARIS, FRlDAY.—Although every effort is being made to bring the work of the Suez Canal Commission to a speedy conclusion, it is progressing but slowly, and much time is lost over discussion of details. At the present moment the question of the liability of the Governmsnts for the damage caused in the canal by their war vessels is still under dis- cussion. It is stated that the Russian and French Govern- ments display great anxiety for bringing the work of the Commission to a speedy conclusion. In the event of the outbreak of war between England and Russia the Commis- sion would at once break up.
THE SOUDAN CAMPAIGN. REBELS SURPRISED BY AN AMBUSH.

The Daily Chronicle publishes the following, dated Souakim, Thursday evening :—With a view to check the annoyance caused by the night attacks of small bodies of rebels, a portion of the 70th regiment went out yesterday afternoon, and formed an ambush in the neighbourhood of Handoub. The expectation that the rebels would renew their attempt to injure the railway was justified by events. About dusk some two hundred rebels passed in a body right along the front of our ambushed men A warm fire was immediately opened on the enemy, who were so scantal at this unexpected reception that they made no at- tempt to fight, and fled across the hills. Our men fired carefully and evidently with affect, for nutnerous traces of blood were found, indicating that a considerable number of the rebels had been hit. As usual, however, they succeeded in carrying off their wounded and dead, if any. Our men are in good spirits at the success of their manceuvre, and hope that it will not be the last occasion on which the enemy will be met with their own tactics.

div.head: EI E WAR CRISIS
div.p: EI E WAR CRISIS
THE PROPOSED ARBITRATION.

• We (Standard) are able to state upon unquestionable authority the present position of the Afghan dispute. The proposal of Mr. Gladstone's Cabinet is that Russia and England should agree to submit to the arbitration of some one of the crowned heads of Europe the simple question whether the arrangement of the 17th of March has been broken by Russia. This proposal is now under the consider- ation of tha Government of the Czar, and it has been de- cided to convoke a meeting of the Committee of Ministers at Gatschina to consider the question. , RUSSIAN GARRISONS IN ASIA.

Sr. PETERSBURG, FRIDAY.—An order of the Minister of War, dated the 19th ultimo, directs the formation of a company of troops at Kragnovodsk, Askabad, and Clukish- kan respectively. to serve as permanent garrisons in those places. A STARTLING STATEMENT.

It is stated that an unexpected difficulty has arisen which affects our relations with the Ameer, and may alter the whole complexion of the Afghan crisis. It Is alleged that the Ameer now declares that Herat is not in his territory, and that be is not anxious to retain it.
The Ameer of Afghanistan; it should be stated on the other hand, is gazetted Hon. Knight Grand Commander of the Star of India. - - -
BRITISH PREPARATIONS.

Orders have been received at the dockyard to enter 200 shipwrights and an indefinite number of joiners and smiths. The new 81-ton gun for H.M.S. Inflexible has arrived here, and will be mounted without delay. Six Nordenfeldt and foe Gardner guns are ordered to the Lord Warden. Ar- rangemente have been directed to enable the Hercules and Sultan to carry two torpedo bests each. The Admiralty have hired the Guion Line steamer Abyssinia, as well as a large steamer of the Allan Line, for the conveyance of troops. The powerful steam tag Indra, which has been pur- chased at Dundee by the Admiralty, is being fitted out few sea and will be ready in three weeks. She will be supplied with two guns, and be employed as a despatch and gun boat. She will also be of service in towing disabled ves•els Out of action. Orders for war material continue to be distributed among the manufacturers of South Staffordshire. An order for 200,000 ramrods for cleaning rifles has been placed with one firm by the British Government, and the greater portion of the steel is to be got from Sheffield. Agents for Russian houses are likewise baying large quantities of articles. _ . _

Orders haye been received at Sheerness directing "num- ber ninety-three" torpedo boat to be Immediately prepared for commission. "Number four" torpedo boat will be ready to leave the Medway on Monday next to join the torpedo Flotilla, attached to the Hada at Ports- mouth. Her Majesty's corvette Roby, twelve guns, was undecked at Sheerness on Friday afternoon upon the com- pletion of her refit, and steamed to Black Stakes to take in her powder and shell. The turret ship Ajtx, four guns, Captain Kennedy, is to be manned with a crew of HO officers and men.

div.head: MEDITERRANEAN STATIONS.
div.p: THE MEDITERRANEAN STATIONS.

In order to put the Mediterranean stations in as perfect a condition as possible, in view of the important position which they would occupy in case of war with Russia, the governors of Gibraltar and Malta have been invited to send home requisitions for all stores which they may require, and their demands:are now receiving the foremost attention at the hands of the War Office. The requisitions are not heavy, both Malta and Gibraltar having of late years been well provided for. The forts and batteries have been re- armed with modern ordnance, and the store-houses filled with war material of all kinds. Several shiploads of fresh sores will, however, be sent out, and yesterday six barges filled with guns and shell went from the Royal Arsenal to the docks for conveyance to Malta alene, that island, which contains the largest reserve of all the naval and military depots abroad, having always the first claim for considera- tion. From Gibraltar Sir John Adaye has sent to Woolwich a large quantity of obsolete guns to make room for new weapons, which will be at once issued, both for the defence of the rock and the refitting of any ships which my be driven into port for repairs. Smaller depots will also, it occasion requires, be established at Cyprus, Suez, and Aden. Already large supplies of fuel have keen sent to Ascension and the other coaling stations. COMMERCIAL PATRIOTISM.

The Press Association's Newcastle correspondent under- stands that the directors of one of the largest mutual steam- ship insurance clubs in the north of England have passed a' recommendation urging their members to bihd themselves notito charter any of their steamers to or from Russian ports during the present month. This would effect between one and two hundred steamers. VOLUNTEER OFFICERS WANTED. On Friday nuornin an order was received at the head- quarters of the Sheffield Volunteers stating that any volun- teer officer who desired may join the regular army for active service. Notices were at once issued by the adjutant of the regiment to the officers to this effect.

It is stated that Mr. Mitchell Henry, M.P., will no again seek election to Parliament on account of failing health, Lady Hawkshaw, wire of Sir John Hawkshaw, C.E , died on Wednesday night, at her residence, Holly Combe, near Peterefleld. ASSAULTING A CcI..NiSTITILE AT WINIVICIC.—John Bag• lev, of Warrington, was charged on remand at the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday, with being drunk in charge of a horse and cart, and also with assaulting P.C. Parker at iNinwick, on the 21st 01r,—P.C. Parker stated that at half-past nine on the previous Tuesday night he saw the prisoner drunk while in charge of a horse and cart at Winwick. He spoke to the man, who began to boat the pony it a savage manner, and on witness trying to got into the cart, the prisoner gave him a severe kick on the breast,—The prisoner was fined 5e and costs for the drunkenness, and 20s land costs for the assault on the office:

LAST NIGHT'S PAIILIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—' Ile Earl of Montan, replying to Lord Harris, said that three militia lieutenants serving with Methuen's Horse in South Africa, had received commis- sions in line regimezts at the Cape.—Lord BURY asked the Government whether, as the vote of credit of eleven mil- lions did not include any provision for further offensive operations in the Soudan, distinct assurance would be given for ensuring safety, and rewarding the services of the Mudir of Dongola and the friendly tribes who joined the British standard at Saakim.—Earl Gneerviu.n, replying, thought, as be had already promised the Marquis of Salis- bury to make a statement of Egyptian policy so soon as the Government thought it consistent with the public ser- vice, he trusted Lord Bury would not think him wanting in politeness if he declined now to answer his queetion.—Earl DERBY, replying to Lord Harris with regard to the settle- ment of the difficulties in Stellaland, South Africa' said Sir Charles Warren had restored order in Bechuanaland, and had met with no armed opposition wherever he had travelled. Further information might be expected before . Whitsuntide. The Australian Federation and Criminal Law Amendment Bills were read a third time, and the House adjourned. . HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. A LONDON RAILWAY B/LL.—On the motion for the second reading of the Regents Canal, City, and Docks Railway Bill, Sir J. PEASE opposed, and, as an amendment, moved that it was not expedient to pass any railway bill which involved the payment of interest out of capital during construction pending the introduction of a public measure on the subject—Sir G. GOULDNEY objected to interfere with people doing what they liked with their own money.—Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the bill was an important one. It would, if passed, give a great amount of employ- ment to labour, and he did not think it would be right to Interfere with that desirable object.—After along discussion the amendment was negatived by 187 to 117, and the bill was read a second time. QUESTIONS.—Mr. Cnoss, replying to Dr. Cameron, said telegrams had been sent to India inquiring whether glan- ders prevailed in the 6th Bengal Lancers, but an answer had not yet been received —Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN, replying to Mr. Healy, said a statement would be made on Monday with regard te the renumeration the Local Go- vernment proposed to give poor law officials under the Registration Bill.—Mr. GLADSTONE, replying to a question, said on Monday it would be stated what decision had been arrived at regarding the throwing expenses of tha Registration Bill on the Consolidated Fund. It was pro- posed to take the report of the vote of credit on Monday.— Mr. Gratosroens, replying to Sir S. Nerthcote, said there was nothing fresh that day regarding the Afghanistan frontier. Damn REGISTRATION.—The House went In committee on the Registration of Voters (Ireland) Bill. , The remaining clauses of the bill were agreed to without amendment; the new clauses were then proceeded with.—Mr. CAMPBELL BANNERMAN proposed a new clause giving the Lord-Lieu- tenant power to appoint additional revising barristers —Mr. HEALY said there was no need to appoint additional revis- ing barristers in southern counties, as there were no pros- pects of contests. As regarded Dublin and Ulster, he hoped that the names of persons proposed to be appointed should be given, so that it might seem that tie appointments were not given for political services.—Mr. Ginsote felt certain that proper persons would be aopointed.—Mr. CAMPBELL BAN- NERMAN assured hon, members there was no intention of doing anything unfair. Additional revising barristers would only be appointed where necessary.—After discussion the clause was agreed to.—A Kew clause, moved by Mr. CAMP- BELL•BANNERMAN, providing that informalities in registra- tion should not affect the validity of register, and for col- lectors giving assistance in serving notices, was agreed to.— Mr. HEALY moved a clause providing that separate rating should not be necessary for household qualiacation, and it was agreed to.—Mr. SMALL moved a clause for dividing boroughs into polling districts.—After discussion the clause was rejected by 80 1029.—Mr. Dimon moved a new clause for the prevention of frivolous objections, and Mr. Camp- bell-Bannerman accepted it.—New clauses were moved by Mr. HEALY, giving power to the Revising Barrister to sum- mon witnesses' and relating to the cost of appeal and duties and powers of Court of Revision, which were agreed to.— Mr. HEALY moved a new clause providing that no students occupying rooms in college for collegiate purposes should be entitled to be registered to vote as lodgers. He pointed out that etudents were not so registered at either Oxford or Cambridge. Mr. CAMPBELL-BANNERMAN was averse to disfranchising anyone, and could see no reason why the student's name should not be upon the register if they possessed the lodger qualification. —Mr. PARNELL supported the clause, and Mr. GIBSON op- posed it, as an attempt to remove 200 voters opposed to Home Rule from the electorial roll in Dublin.—After a long discussion the clause was rejected by 127 to 31 votes. —Mr. SEXTON moved a new clause enacing the punishment for clerks of unions for delaying or refusing the perfor- mance of the duties, which was agreed to after the word " wilfully " had been inserted. I' Liner ammo.]

div.head: MAY DAY PROCESSION AT WIDNES.
div.p: MAY DAY PROCESSION AT WIDNES.

Although the centre of an industry which blights and withers vegetation within a circle of several miles, Widnes, incongruous as it may seem, celebrates the advent of the month of flowers by a procession of gaily bedecked horses and conveyances. In fact, an association was formed six years ago for the purpose of maintaining the ancient cus- tom, and yesterday the procession showed a perceptible im- provement on previous years. Prins were offered for the best, neatest, and cleanest turnout in a variety of classes, and the competitors numbered about 30. The judging took place on a piece of-waste ground near the Norton Arms Hotel, which is the headquarters of the association, and the awards were as follows:

MANUFACTURER, DOUBLE DRAUGHT HORSES. -- Messrs. Muspratt and Sons; 2nd. Mr. W. Smith, iron- founder, Legsdale ; 3rd, Widnes Foundry Company. MANUFACTURERS SINGLE DRAUGHT HORSRS.-1, Mr. Pster Longton, Spring Brewery, Bitten ; 2 and 3, Widnes Local Board.
MANUFACTURERS DOUBLE COBS.-1, Mr. T. Edwardson, mineral water manufacturer, Simms Cross. _ . _ _
MANUFACTURERS SIiH COBS-1, Widnes Local Board; 2, P. Longton. CoNTSACTORS AWD CAST OWNERS SINGLE DRAUGHT HORSES.-1, Mr. J. Norris; 2, Mr. E. Percy, Victoria. street.

CONTRACTORS AND CAW OWNERS SINOLB COBS.-1, Mr. J. Hulme, coal dealer ; 2, Mrs Elizabeth Hulmo. TRADESMEN'S, 13 RAND, OR OVHR —lSt, Mr. W. Far. rant, grocer, Waterloo-road ; 2nd, Mr. C. Hemingway, Charch-street; 3rd, Mr. W. Palin, grocer. Ann-street. Postvs —lst, Mr. R. Smithson, contractor, Lngsdale; 2nd, Mr. S. J. Francis. DONKEYS —let, Mr. Francis

Messrs. W. Turton, Burnt Mill Farm, Halewood ; John Kenwright, Tarbock Hall; and William Berry, Ditton, ably officiated as judges. About half-past two the procession started, the dark clouds which had been hovering overhead all morning at the earns time commenced to rain, and the tour of the town was made in a damp and chilling atmo- sphere. The event, howesnor,.excited considerable interest, especially among the younger portion of the population, and many of the animals were in tine condition and excited the admiration of the spectators. The Widnes Local Board took advantage of the occasion to advertise their gas cook- ing stoves, a couple of which were placed upon a newly- painted cart, drawn by a handsome and gaily decorated animal.

She and a younger sister were playing with each other, when the latt.r accidentally bit her sister with an umbrella, the point of which entered one of her eves, com- pletely destroying sight. SCHOOL OF Aux.—Theannual examinations in connection with South Kensington are now proceeding. Oa Wednes- day 59 students sat for-model drawing. 61 for freehand, and 5 for advanced perspective (theory). On Thursday 277 sat for geometry, 29 ,for perspective (3rd grade), and 5 for ad- vanced perspective (practical); and last night 7 sat for advanced model drawing, WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. On Sunday evening another of the special pimple's services was held in this church, and-was attended by a large congregation. The Rev. J. Yonge occupied the pulpit and preached from the text "If any man thirst let rim come unto me and drink." At the close of the discourses Miss Wallington sang:iaavery effective manner the hymn "Come unto me." UNITED KINGDO6I BAND OF HOPES Eixtow.--Among the successful candidates in the annual examination for the Warrington centre of this Union, held in February last, we notice the name of William Arthur Stone, of the Silver- street Band of Hope. There were over 3006 h oatedidates, and 200-prizes were awarded. Ho has won one of the best prizes, being third in all England in his years CONSERVATIVE MEETING AT CROFT.—On Friday evening a meeting of the Conservatives of the Soothworth- with-Croft district of the Newton Division of South-West Lancashire was held at the Beard School, Croft, to elect five representatives on the Conservative Council for the above disttict. There was only a moderate attendance. The chair was occupied By Mr. Reginald Owen, sen. Mr. Woodnorth kindly explained the objector the seeeting, after which the following persons were appointed, namely, ,Mears. Reginald Owen, see, Henry Percy Dodson, James Hunt, Samuel Thomason, and Jahn Daintlth. Mr. Owen„ sen., was also elected to serve on the Executive Corn- mittee, _ _

WARRINGTON FARMERS' CLDII —A meeting of the cam-. mittee of this club was held on Wednesday afternoon in the clubroom, White Ball Inn, Horsemarket-street. There was a good attendance of members. It was stated by the Secre- tary (Mr. H. F. Htelfox). that at the first meeting of the club the Mayor of Wasrington (Alderman Harriszt),, Dr, Mackie, and Mr. Jeans had been proposed as members of the club, but subsequently objected to by some of the mem- bers as not being tenant farmers. It was for the committee to say whether or not they should be members. After some oonverration it was agreed, that these gentlemen should be accepted as members, The subsequent lousiness of the meeting was the consideration of a plan far active operations for the club, and gentlemen were selected to read papers Lod to open debates on various subjects =netted with the. ag- ricultural iaterto,

THiI SOUDN CAMPATGN. PROBABLE WITHDRAWAL OF THE TROOPS. SUAKIM, Beamatnaa.—Spies report that Osman Dig,ma is at Tenni with 200 followers. Iler Majesty's treopship Jumna bas arrived here with I,2oocoolieson board. Stumm, STYNDAY.—GeneraI Graham bas received a long despatch from Lord Wolseley, containing definite instruc- tions. ' The actual contents of the despatch have not tran- ' spired. It is understood, however, that at a meeting of the principal naval, military, and civil authorities to-day, the early withdrawal of the troops was announced. The medical officials are strongly in favour of an immediate withdrawal. DONGOLA, SATURDAY —Reports have reached here con- firming the defeat of the Mandi's troops in Kordofan. Abou Anga, one of the Mandi's lieutenants, was killed. The troops at Omdurman are wavering in their allegiance to the Mandi. A paper emanating from an orthodox Mussulman, refuting the alandi's claim., is being cir- culated among the native population, by whom it ie largely read. DONCF)LA, MONDAY —The Mandi's troops Are reported to have been defeated by the Senaar garrison. Smallpox is raging at Omdurman. DONGOLA, TUESDAY.—CoI. Grant, of the Royal Engineers, has arrived here from England. Spies report that all the artisans employed in the arsenal at Khartoum were killed at the capture of that place, and that consequently no car- tridges have been manufactured since that time. Snaxtm, TUESDAY.—The tranaport Australia will leave to-morrow for Portsmouth with a number of invalids and a portion of the Royal Marines. DAMAGING THE RAILWAY. SUAKIM, WEDNESDAY.—Last night a number of the Iladendowas again damaged the railway. They burned a number of the sleepers, and carried aw ty many of the iron fish plates, as well as several of the iron ends of the tele- graph poles. This mischief was done at a paint about two miles distant from the headquarters camp. This morning a reconnaissance was made from Han,lub to Theraubert,w hich is a place some six miles up the llasheen Valley. The troops saw none of the enemy, although it was perfectly evident that they had been at the place in last night in large numbers. LORD WOLSELEY. CAIRO, NVEDNRSDAY.—Lord Wolseley, accompanied by his staff, left here for Bnakim this morning. Lie is expected to return hereon the 11th proximo.
